title: LPIC-2 Exam 202 (202-450) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from LPI's public LPIC-2 Exam 202 (202-450) objectives, version 4.5 only (https://www.lpi.org/our-certifications/exam-201-202-objectives/, checked 2026-11-27). Not real exam questions. The real exam has 60 questions in 90 minutes; this bank has a larger pool and 6 hands-on items, and draws an exam by the official topic weights. Practice only on your own lab machines or VMs, never on systems you do not have written permission to change or test.

q.q: You edited /etc/bind/named.conf.local on a Debian BIND 9 server and want to find syntax mistakes BEFORE you reload anything. Which command does that?
o: named-checkzone example.com /etc/bind/named.conf.local
named-checkzone tests a zone data file, not the main configuration. Pointed at a config file it only reports nonsense.
rndc reconfig
This tells the RUNNING server to load the new config. It does not check anything first, so an error can break the live server.
rndc status
It shows version, number of zones and boot time of the running server. It never reads the config files you edited.
named-checkconf
Right. named-checkconf reads named.conf and every file it includes, and prints the line of any syntax error. It does not touch the running server.

q.q: You added a new zone block to named.conf. You want named to start serving ONLY the new zone, without re-reading the zones it already serves. Which command fits best?
o: rndc flush
flush empties the resolver cache. It does not read named.conf at all.
rndc reconfig
Right. reconfig re-reads named.conf and loads zones that are new, but it does not reload zones that are already loaded. It is the light-touch way to add a zone.
rndc retransfer example.com
This forces a secondary to pull a fresh copy of one zone from its primary. It does not add a zone that is missing from the config.
rndc reload
reload re-reads the config AND every zone file, which the question rules out.

q.q: ns2 must be a secondary (slave) for example.com. The primary is 192.0.2.10. Which zone block on ns2 is correct for BIND 9?
o: zone "example.com" { type secondary; primaries { 192.0.2.10; }; file "db.example.com"; };
Right. type secondary (older name: slave) plus the primaries list (older name: masters) makes ns2 pull the zone by AXFR/IXFR and save it to the file.
zone "example.com" { type forward; forwarders { 192.0.2.10; }; };
A forward zone sends QUERIES to another resolver. It never copies zone data, so ns2 would not be authoritative for the zone.
zone "example.com" { type hint; file "db.example.com"; };
type hint is only for the root zone ("."). It loads the list of root servers.
zone "example.com" { type primary; allow-transfer { 192.0.2.10; }; file "db.example.com"; };
This makes ns2 a second primary. allow-transfer controls who may copy the zone FROM ns2; it does not make ns2 copy from 192.0.2.10.

q.q: A caching resolver on 10.1.0.53 must answer recursive queries only for the internal range 10.1.0.0/16, so outsiders cannot use it in DNS amplification attacks. Which option in the options block does this?
o: allow-transfer { 10.1.0.0/16; }; (inside options)
allow-transfer decides who may download a whole zone with AXFR. It has no effect on recursion.
allow-update { 10.1.0.0/16; }; (inside the zone)
allow-update lets listed hosts change a zone with dynamic DNS updates. It is a risky setting and not a recursion control.
allow-recursion { 10.1.0.0/16; };
Right. allow-recursion limits who may ask the server to look up names on their behalf. Outsiders still get answers for zones the server is authoritative for.
listen-on picks the server's own addresses to bind to. It does not filter which CLIENTS may use recursion.

q.q: You run dig @192.0.2.53 www.example.com. The header shows "flags: qr rd ra" and there is no "aa" flag. What does the missing aa flag tell you?
o: The zone's serial number is too low, so the answer is out of date
The serial number is inside the SOA record. It never appears as a flag in the header.
It is not authoritative: the answer came from the cache or another server
Right. aa means Authoritative Answer. It is set only when the server answers from a zone it owns. Cached or recursed answers do not carry it.
Recursion is switched off on that server, so it only answers from its own zones
ra (recursion available) IS present in the flags, so recursion is on. The aa flag is about who owns the data.
The reply was truncated and the client must retry over TCP because it did not fit in one UDP packet
Truncation sets the tc flag. A missing aa flag has nothing to do with message size.

q.q: A small office wants ONE light program that gives its clients DNS forwarding with a local cache, reads /etc/hosts for local names and can also hand out DHCP leases. Which software matches?
o: PowerDNS
PowerDNS is a full authoritative server (often with database back ends) plus a separate recursor. It has no DHCP server.
djbdns
djbdns is a set of separate tools (tinydns for authoritative data, dnscache for caching). It does not include DHCP.
dnsmasq
Right. dnsmasq is a small DNS forwarder/cache with a built-in DHCP server. It is common on routers and small networks.
BIND 9
BIND is the reference DNS server for both authoritative and recursive use. DHCP is a separate program (ISC dhcpd).

q.q: Only the file db.example.com changed on the primary. You raised the serial and want only that zone reloaded. Which command does it?
o: rndc reconfig example.com
reconfig takes no zone name. It only re-reads named.conf and loads new zones.
rndc flushname example.com
flushname removes cached records for that name. It does not read any zone file.
rndc freeze example.com
freeze stops dynamic updates so you can edit a dynamic zone by hand. It does not load the changed file.
rndc reload example.com
Right. reload with a zone name re-reads just that zone's file, and the server then sends NOTIFY to its secondaries.

q.q: You edited db.example.com on the primary and added a host, but the secondary DNS server still returns old data an hour later. The file has no syntax errors and named reloaded fine. What did you most likely forget?
o: To increase the serial number in the SOA record
Right. Secondaries compare the serial number from the primary with their own copy. Only a higher serial makes them transfer the zone.
To restart the secondary's named service after every change
A restart is not needed. The secondary pulls data by itself when the primary's serial is higher.
To set the SOA refresh value to 0
A refresh of 0 would cause constant polling or invalid timing. It does not force a transfer, and the serial is what is compared.
To end every host name in the zone file with a dot
A trailing dot matters only for fully qualified names. Missing dots cause wrong names, not an unchanged zone.

q.q: You must create the reverse zone for the network 192.0.2.0/24. What is the correct zone name in named.conf?
o: 192.0.2.in-addr.arpa
The octets must be reversed. This name would belong to the network 2.0.192.0/24.
2.0.192.in-addr.arpa
Right. Reverse zones list the network octets in reverse order and end in in-addr.arpa. The three network octets 192.0.2 become 2.0.192.
0.2.192.in-addr.arpa
This name is wrongly ordered and has an extra octet. It would be for the network 192.2.0.0/24.
arpa.in-addr.2.0.192
The parts of the name are in the wrong order. Reverse names always end in in-addr.arpa.

q.q: In the reverse zone 2.0.192.in-addr.arpa, which line correctly maps 192.0.2.25 to mail.example.com?
o: 25 IN PTR mail.example.com.
Right. Inside the reverse zone only the last octet is needed. The target is a fully qualified name, so it ends with a dot.
25 IN PTR mail.example.com
Without the final dot, named adds the zone name, and the target becomes mail.example.com.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa.
mail IN PTR 192.0.2.25.
A PTR record is written the other way round: the address label is on the left, the host name on the right.
25.2.0.192 IN PTR mail.example.com.
The zone name is added to the left side, giving 25.2.0.192.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa, which is not the intended name.

q.q: named-checkzone reports: "www.example.com: CNAME and other data". What is wrong in the zone file?
o: The CNAME target name is missing its final dot in the file
A missing dot makes the target a wrong name, but named-checkzone would not call it "other data".
The SOA serial number is older than the one on the secondary server
named-checkzone does not compare serials with other servers. It only reads the one file.
The zone has no NS records at the top (apex) of the zone file
A missing NS gives a different message ("no NS records"). This message names a conflict at one specific name.
www has a CNAME plus another record type, such as an A or MX record
Right. A CNAME says "this name is an alias for another name", so no other data may exist at that same name.

q.q: Which MX record, placed in the zone file for example.com, is valid AND points mail to the host mail.example.com?
o: @ IN MX mail.example.com.
The preference number is missing, so the file will not load.
An MX target must be a host name, not an IP address. named would read 192.0.2.25 as a relative name inside the zone.
@ IN MX 10 mail.example.com.
Right. An MX record needs a preference number and a fully qualified host name ending in a dot.
@ IN MX 10 mail.example.com
It loads, but with no final dot the target becomes mail.example.com.example.com., which does not exist.

q.q: In the example.com zone you must delegate dev.example.com to its own name server ns1.dev.example.com at 192.0.2.60. What goes in the PARENT zone file?
o: Only an NS record for dev, because the child zone's own file holds the A record
Resolvers could not find ns1.dev without already knowing where dev lives. That loop is why glue is needed in the parent.
Only an A record for ns1.dev, because glue alone is enough to delegate
An A record alone does not delegate anything. Without the NS record, the parent keeps answering for dev itself.
A CNAME for dev pointing to ns1.dev.example.com
A CNAME makes dev an alias for a host. It does not delegate a zone and would block other records at that name.
An NS record for dev to ns1.dev.example.com, plus an A (glue) record for ns1.dev
Right. The NS record hands the sub-zone to the child server. The glue A record is needed because the name server's own name lies inside the zone being delegated.

q.q: Which dig command asks the server 192.0.2.53 for the reverse (PTR) name of 192.0.2.25?
o: This asks for a PTR at the literal name 192.0.2.25, which is not in the reverse tree, so there is no answer.
+trace walks from the root servers and ignores the @server. It also still uses the wrong literal name.
Right. -x builds the in-addr.arpa name for you and asks for the PTR record. @ chooses the server to ask.
The octets are in the right reverse order, but the name lacks the in-addr.arpa suffix, so it is not a reverse name.

q.q: You must reduce the damage if someone finds a bug in BIND and takes over the named process. Which TWO named start options help? (Choose two.)
o: -c /etc/bind/named.conf
-c just names the configuration file to read. It does not limit the process.
-g
-g keeps named in the foreground and sends logs to the terminal. It is for debugging and adds no protection.
-4 makes named use IPv4 only. It changes the network sockets, not what a hijacked process may do.
-t /var/lib/named
Right. -t puts named in a chroot jail. A hijacked process then sees only that folder, not the whole disk.
-u bind
Right. -u makes named drop root rights after it binds port 53 and run as the unprivileged user "bind".

q.q: A secondary ns2 (192.0.2.12) logs: "zone example.com/IN: refused AXFR from 192.0.2.11" ... on the PRIMARY the log says "client 192.0.2.12#41234: zone transfer 'example.com/AXFR/IN' denied". The primary's zone has "allow-transfer { key xfer-key; };" and defines key "xfer-key" with hmac-sha256. What must ns2 add?
o: The same key "xfer-key" block, plus a server 192.0.2.11 { keys xfer-key; }; statement so its requests are TSIG-signed
Right. The primary only accepts transfers signed with the shared key. ns2 needs the same key secret and a server statement that tells named to sign requests to that address.
A DS record for example.com published in the parent zone
DS records link a signed zone to its parent for DNSSEC. They have nothing to do with who may request a transfer.
An allow-transfer { 192.0.2.11; }; line in the zone block on ns2
allow-transfer on ns2 controls who may copy the zone FROM ns2. The denial is on the primary and needs a signed request.
The key secret as a TXT record in the example.com zone file
Publishing a secret in a zone file would give it to the world. TSIG keys stay in named.conf (or a key file) on both servers.

q.q: One BIND server must answer example.com with 10.0.0.5 for internal clients and with 203.0.113.5 for everyone else. How do you build this?
o: Two zone "example.com" statements in the main options block
A zone name may appear only once per view. Without views, named refuses to load the duplicate.
Two view blocks with match-clients, each with its own example.com zone
Right. Views let one server show different data to different clients. The first view whose match-clients fits the client is used, so list the internal one first.
One zone file with two A records for www, one for each of the two networks
That is round robin: every client sees both addresses. It cannot choose by who is asking.
allow-query { 10.0.0.0/8; }; inside the single example.com zone block
allow-query only lets or blocks clients. It cannot return different data.

q.q: example.com is DNSSEC-signed. To build the chain of trust, which record must the .com registry publish in the PARENT zone?
o: An RRSIG record for the whole zone
RRSIG records are signatures and live inside the child zone next to the data they sign.
A DNSKEY record for example.com
DNSKEY is the public key. It is published in the signed child zone, and the parent only holds its hash (DS).
A DS record
Right. A DS (delegation signer) record holds a hash of the child's key-signing key. Resolvers use it to trust the child's DNSKEY.
A TLSA record
TLSA is for DANE and ties a TLS certificate to a service name. It does not link zones together.

q.q: A mail admin wants clients to check a mail server's TLS certificate against information published in DNS, not only against public CAs. Which record type does DANE use for this?
o: TLSA
Right. A TLSA record stores a certificate (or hash of it) for a given port and host name. It is only safe when the zone is DNSSEC-signed.
SRV
SRV tells clients which host and port offer a service. It carries no certificate data.
CAA
CAA says which certificate authorities may issue certificates for a domain. It does not let a client check a certificate directly.
SSHFP
SSHFP holds fingerprints of SSH host keys, not TLS certificates.

q.q: In Apache 2.4 you must let only the network 10.5.0.0/16 open /var/www/admin. Which directive inside the Directory block does this?
o: Allow from 10.5.0.0/16
This is Apache 2.2 syntax. It only works if mod_access_compat is loaded, and it needs Order lines too.
Require ip 10.5.0.0/16
Right. Require is the Apache 2.4 way (mod_authz_core). Clients outside the range get 403.
Require host 10.5.0.0/16
Require host expects a host or domain NAME such as .example.com, not a network range.
Require local 10.5.0.0/16
Require local takes no argument; it means only the server's own addresses.

q.q: A .htaccess file in /var/www/html/app contains Redirect rules, but Apache ignores them completely and logs no error. Which setting is the usual cause?
o: Options -Indexes set in the main config for the whole site
That only turns off folder listings. It does not stop .htaccess files from being read.
KeepAlive Off set in the main config for every virtual host
KeepAlive controls reuse of TCP connections. It has no link to .htaccess.
DirectoryIndex is missing for that folder in the vhost
DirectoryIndex picks the default page. Without it you may see a listing or 403, but .htaccess is still read.
AllowOverride None for that directory in the main config
Right. AllowOverride says which directives a .htaccess file may use. With None, Apache does not even look for the file.

q.q: Apache serves two name-based virtual hosts on 192.0.2.10:80. A request arrives with the Host header "unknown.example.net", which matches no ServerName or ServerAlias. Which site answers?
o: The main server config that sits outside every VirtualHost block
Once a VirtualHost exists for an address and port, the main config no longer answers requests for it.
The virtual host with the longest ServerName
Length plays no role. Apache matches by exact name or alias, and then falls back to the first block.
The first virtual host defined for 192.0.2.10:80
Right. The first matching VirtualHost block acts as the default for that address and port when nothing else matches.
None; Apache returns 400 Bad Request
A Host header with an unknown name is still valid HTTP. Apache simply serves the default (first) host.

q.q: Which line permanently redirects every request for /old to https://www.example.com/new using mod_alias?
o: Alias /old https://www.example.com/new with status 301
Alias maps a URL to a path on the local disk. A full URL as the target is not a valid file path.
ErrorDocument 301 https://www.example.com/new for /old
ErrorDocument sets the page shown for an error code. It does not send redirects for a path.
DirectoryIndex https://www.example.com/new
DirectoryIndex lists default file names for a folder, nothing about redirecting.
Redirect permanent /old https://www.example.com/new
Right. Redirect with "permanent" sends HTTP 301, which tells browsers and search engines the move is lasting.

q.q: /etc/apache2/.htpasswd already holds the user alice. You must add the user bob without losing alice. Which command is right?
o: htpasswd /etc/apache2/.htpasswd bob
Right. Without -c, htpasswd adds the user (or updates a password) in the existing file.
htpasswd -c /etc/apache2/.htpasswd bob
-c CREATES the file, so it overwrites it. alice would be gone.
htpasswd -D /etc/apache2/.htpasswd bob
-D deletes a user from the file.
htdigest /etc/apache2/.htpasswd realm bob
htdigest builds a different file format for Digest authentication, not for the Basic .htpasswd file.

q.q: A protected folder has AuthType Basic, AuthName "Staff" and AuthUserFile set correctly, but visitors get in without any password prompt. Which line is missing?
o: AuthGroupFile /dev/null
That only tells Apache there is no group file. It never forces a login.
Require valid-user
Right. The Auth* lines only describe HOW to authenticate. Require is what makes Apache demand and check a login.
Satisfy all
Satisfy was a 2.2 directive. In 2.4 it does not replace a Require line.
LimitRequestBody 0
It controls the maximum size of the request body and has no link to authentication.

q.q: In the "combined" access log format, which two extra fields are recorded compared to the "common" format?
o: The server's response time and the vhost name
Those need custom fields such as %D or %v. Neither belongs to the combined format.
The Referer and the User-Agent
Right. combined = common + "%{Referer}i" + "%{User-agent}i". They help to see where visitors came from and what browser they used.
The SSL protocol and cipher suite
Those need %{SSL_PROTOCOL}x style fields in a custom format, they are not in combined.
The authenticated user and the request size
Both of these are already in the common format (the user and the bytes sent).

q.q: An Apache server on mpm_prefork starts so many child processes under load that it runs out of memory and swaps. Which directive sets the maximum number of simultaneous requests the server will handle?
o: KeepAliveTimeout 5
It sets how long an idle persistent connection stays open. It does not cap workers.
LimitRequestBody 1048576
It limits the size of one request body (for uploads), not the number of requests.
ListenBacklog 1024
It sets the length of the queue of pending connections in the kernel and does not limit running workers.
MaxRequestWorkers
Right. In Apache 2.4 it caps simultaneous requests (older name: MaxClients). Lower it so the processes fit in RAM.

q.q: Apache uses the event MPM (threaded). You must run PHP pages safely. Which setup is the usual choice?
o: mod_php loaded into every thread of the event MPM server
mod_php needs the non-threaded prefork MPM in practice, because common PHP builds are not thread-safe.
mod_perl with a PHP handler set through SetHandler perl-script, which then loads php
mod_perl embeds the Perl interpreter. It cannot run PHP code.
php-fpm behind mod_proxy_fcgi, using a SetHandler for .php files
Right. PHP runs in separate FPM processes and Apache passes requests over FastCGI. This works with threaded MPMs.
Plain CGI where each .php page begins with a #!/bin/sh line, so Apache runs it as a shell script
CGI can run scripts but PHP files need the PHP interpreter, and CGI is slow. It is not the usual setup.

q.q: Before applying changes to the Apache config on a live production-like lab server, which command checks the syntax without stopping the service?
o: apachectl configtest
Right. configtest (same as apachectl -t) parses the config and prints "Syntax OK" or the first error. The running server is untouched.
apachectl graceful-stop
It stops the server after current requests end. That would take the site down.
apachectl status
It shows the mod_status page (if enabled) with activity. It does not parse the config files.
apachectl -S -k restart
-S lists vhost settings, but -k restart would restart the server with the new config even if it has errors.

q.q: Which single openssl command creates a new RSA private key AND a certificate signing request (CSR) without prompting for a key passphrase?
o: openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -out www.key -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:2048
This makes only the private key. You would still need openssl req to create the CSR.
openssl x509 -req -in www.csr -signkey www.key -out www.crt
x509 -req turns an existing CSR into a certificate. It needs the CSR first.
openssl s_client -connect www.example.com:443 -showcerts
s_client tests a remote TLS server. It does not create keys or requests.
openssl req -new -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout www.key -out www.csr
Right. req -new builds the CSR, -newkey makes the key at the same time, -nodes leaves the key unencrypted.

q.q: A lab site uses a certificate made with "openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048". Browsers say "Not secure", and "openssl s_client -connect lab1:443" ends with "verify error:num=18:self-signed certificate". What does this error mean, and what is the real fix for users outside the lab?
o: The certificate is its own issuer and no trusted CA signed it; install a certificate from a trusted CA (or import your lab CA into the clients)
Right. Error 18 means the chain ends in a certificate that signed itself and is not in the client's trust store. A trusted CA, or a lab CA that clients trust, solves that.
The intermediate certificate is missing; add it with SSLCertificateChainFile
A missing intermediate gives a different error (num=20 or 21, unable to get local issuer certificate). Here the server's own certificate is the root.
The key is too short; regenerate it with rsa:4096
Key length is not the problem. A 4096-bit self-signed certificate gives the same error 18.
The certificate has expired; renew it for another 365 days
An expired certificate gives error 10 (certificate has expired). A new self-signed one would still be untrusted.

q.q: Your HTTPS site works on desktop browsers, but some phones and Java programs say "unable to verify the first certificate". openssl s_client shows only one certificate in the chain sent by the server. What is wrong?
o: The private key file does not match the server certificate file
A key mismatch would stop Apache from starting with SSL, for every client.
SNI is switched off on the server, so the wrong site is shown
A missing SNI gives the wrong certificate for the name, not a missing chain.
The intermediate CA certificate is not sent by the server
Right. Desktop browsers may fetch or cache the intermediate, but many clients do not. Add the intermediate to the certificate file (Apache 2.4.8+) or to SSLCertificateChainFile.
The certificate is a wildcard certificate, which some clients reject
Major clients accept wildcard certificates. They have no link to missing chain certificates.

q.q: Which Apache line allows only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3?
o: SSLCipherSuite TLSv1.2:TLSv1.3
SSLCipherSuite selects ciphers by name, not protocol versions. TLS version names are not cipher names.
SSLProtocol -all +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3
Right. -all first removes every protocol, then each + adds one back. This leaves only the two modern versions.
SSLProtocol all -SSLv3 -SSLv2 -TLSv1
This still allows TLS 1.1, which is outdated. Only 1.2 and 1.3 should stay.
SSLEngine optional TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3
SSLEngine takes on, off or optional. It switches SSL on or off for the vhost.

q.q: You host three HTTPS sites with three different certificates on ONE IP address and port 443, using name-based virtual hosts. Which TLS feature makes that possible?
o: HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security)
HSTS is a header that tells browsers to use HTTPS only. It does not help pick a certificate.
SNI (Server Name Indication)
Right. The client sends the host name in the TLS handshake before the certificate is chosen, so Apache can pick the right one.
OCSP stapling of the certificate status
Stapling attaches a fresh revocation answer to the handshake. It does not choose between certificates.
ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation)
ALPN picks the application protocol, such as h2 or http/1.1, not the certificate.

q.q: You want to see exactly which certificates your own lab server sends for the name www.example.test, including the chain. Which command does that?
o: openssl verify -CAfile ca.pem www.example.test:443
verify checks a certificate FILE against a CA file. It does not connect to a server.
openssl x509 -in https://192.0.2.10:443 -noout -text -servername www.example.test
x509 reads local files, not URLs.
openssl s_client -connect 192.0.2.10:443 -servername www.example.test -showcerts
Right. s_client opens a TLS session, -servername sends SNI, and -showcerts prints each certificate in the chain.
openssl req -in 192.0.2.10:443 -noout -text -servername www.example.test
req works with certificate signing requests in files, not live servers.

q.q: Browsers keep starting at http://shop.example.test, so every first visit costs a redirect. The port 80 virtual host already has "Redirect permanent / https://shop.example.test/". "curl -sI https://shop.example.test | grep -i strict" prints nothing. Which change makes returning browsers go straight to HTTPS?
o: Add Header always set Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000" to the port 443 virtual host (mod_headers enabled)
Right. Browsers accept HSTS only from an HTTPS response. They then remember to use HTTPS for that host for max-age seconds.
Add the same Strict-Transport-Security header to the port 80 virtual host only
Browsers ignore HSTS sent over plain HTTP, so it would never be stored.
Change the port 80 line to "Redirect temp / https://shop.example.test/"
A temporary redirect (302) is followed once and never remembered by the browser.
Add SSLRequireSSL to the port 80 virtual host
SSLRequireSSL rejects non-SSL requests on a vhost that has SSL on. It does not teach browsers anything.

q.q: Which TWO Apache directives must point to files (the key is stored in a separate file) for a basic HTTPS virtual host to start? (Choose two.)
o: SSLPassPhraseDialog
It sets how Apache asks for a key passphrase at start-up. It is not a file path to a certificate or key.
SSLCertificateKeyFile
Right. It points to the private key that matches the certificate. Keep that file readable by root only.
SSLCertificateFile
Right. It points to the server certificate (and, in 2.4.8 and later, may hold the intermediate chain too).
SSLCACertificateFile
It lists CAs used to check CLIENT certificates, only needed with client certificate authentication.
SSLSessionCache
It sets where TLS session data is cached. It improves speed but is not required for a vhost to start.

q.q: In squid.conf you have: "acl lan src 10.0.0.0/8", "http_access deny all", "http_access allow lan" (in this order). Staff on 10.0.0.0/8 all get TCP_DENIED. Why?
o: ACLs have to be defined below the http_access lines that use them, and this one is above
ACLs must be defined BEFORE any http_access line that uses them, so their place is correct here.
src ACLs only work with IPv6 addresses, so the IPv4 range never matches
src works with IPv4 and IPv6 networks.
Squid needs http_port 80 instead of the default 3128 before allow rules work
The port setting is separate. Squid uses 3128 by default and still processes http_access.
http_access lines run top to bottom and the first match wins, so deny all fires first
Right. The "allow lan" line is never reached. Put specific allow rules before the final deny all.

q.q: You keep a list of banned domains in /etc/squid/blocked.txt, one per line (for example ".badsite.test"). Which pair of lines blocks them for everyone?
o: acl blocked srcdomain "/etc/squid/blocked.txt" and http_access deny blocked, placed above the allow rules for the LAN
srcdomain matches the SOURCE (client) name, not the site that the client wants to reach.
acl blocked dstdomain "/etc/squid/blocked.txt" and http_access deny blocked, placed above the allow rule
Right. dstdomain matches the destination site name, and the quoted file name loads the list. Deny must come first because the first match wins.
acl blocked dst "/etc/squid/blocked.txt" and http_access deny blocked, placed above the allow rules for the LAN
dst matches destination IP addresses. A list of domain names does not fit it.
acl blocked url_regex /etc/squid/blocked.txt and http_access allow blocked, placed above the allow rule
Allow would permit the listed sites instead of blocking them, and url_regex would read the file name as a pattern.

q.q: Squid must make users log in before browsing, using an htpasswd-style file. Which ACL type makes http_access demand a login?
o: ident (user name lookup)
ident asks the client's ident daemon for a user name, which is old and easy to fake. It is not a password login.
srcdomain (client name)
srcdomain matches the client's DNS name. No user name or password is involved.
time (hours of the day)
A time ACL matches hours and days. It cannot ask for credentials.
proxy_auth
Right. "acl users proxy_auth REQUIRED" with "http_access allow users" makes Squid ask for credentials set up by auth_param.

q.q: In squid.conf the line is "cache_dir ufs /var/spool/squid 10000 16 256". What does 10000 mean?
o: The cache holds at most 10000 objects before old ones are removed
Squid limits the disk size in megabytes, not the number of objects.
Cached pages expire after 10000 seconds unless refresh_pattern says otherwise
Expiry depends on refresh_pattern rules and not on cache_dir.
The cache may use up to 10000 megabytes (about 10 GB) of disk
Right. The numbers after the path are: size in MB, number of first-level directories (16) and second-level directories per first-level one (256).
Squid listens on TCP port 10000 for cache requests
The listening port comes from http_port (default 3128).

q.q: You changed squid.conf and want Squid to re-read it without dropping the users' connections. Which command?
o: squid -k reconfigure
Right. It sends the running Squid a signal to re-read its config. Existing connections finish normally.
squid -k shutdown now
It starts a shutdown (after a short wait for clients). The proxy would go away.
squid -k parse -f squid.conf
parse only checks the syntax of squid.conf. The running Squid does not use the result.
squid -k rotate
It rotates the log files. Config is not re-read as part of it.

q.q: Nginx must forward every request for / to an application listening on 127.0.0.1:8080. Which directive inside the location block does this?
o: fastcgi_pass 127.0.0.1:8080;
fastcgi_pass speaks the FastCGI protocol, used for PHP-FPM. A plain HTTP app would not understand it.
upstream app { server 127.0.0.1:8080; }
upstream defines a named group of servers in the http block. By itself it routes nothing.
root sets a folder on disk to serve files from. It is not a network address.
proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080;
Right. proxy_pass hands the request to a backend over HTTP and returns its answer. This is a reverse proxy.

q.q: Behind an nginx reverse proxy, the application's access log shows every visitor as 127.0.0.1. What do you add to the location block so the app can see the real client address?
o: proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
Right. This adds the client address to a header that the app can read. The app must also be set to trust that header from the proxy.
proxy_bind $remote_addr; # use the client's address to reach the backend
proxy_bind sets the local address nginx uses to connect to the backend. It does not tell the app about the client.
real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For; set_real_ip_from 127.0.0.1;
That directive handles addresses nginx RECEIVES from a front proxy. It does not add anything toward the backend.
proxy_redirect http://127.0.0.1:8080/ /;
proxy_redirect rewrites Location headers in backend replies, which is unrelated to client addresses.

q.q: Two server blocks listen on port 80. Neither has a server_name that matches the Host header of an incoming request. Which block answers?
o: The block with the shortest server_name, because nginx prefers short names
Name length is not part of the selection.
The block marked "listen 80 default_server", or the first one if none is marked
Right. Nginx picks by server_name first, then falls back to the default server for that listen address and port.
The block that was read last from the conf.d folder, as the last one replaces the others
Order of reading matters only when no default_server is set, and then the FIRST one wins, not the last.
None, because without a match nginx closes the connection
Nginx always has a default server for a port. It only closes the connection if you use "return 444" in that block.

q.q: After you edit an nginx site file, which sequence safely applies it without breaking active connections?
o: nginx -s stop, then nginx
stop ends the server at once and drops active connections.
nginx -V, then nginx -s quit
-V only prints the version and build options. quit would shut the server down after requests end.
nginx -t, then nginx -s reload
Right. -t checks syntax. -s reload starts new workers with the new config and lets old workers finish their requests.
systemctl mask nginx, then systemctl start nginx
Masking blocks the service from starting at all.

q.q: Nginx has this block: location /img/ { alias /srv/pics/; }. A visitor requests /img/cat.png. Which file does nginx serve?
o: /srv/pics/img/cat.png
That would happen with root /srv/pics;, which APPENDS the whole URI to the folder.
/img/cat.png
Without a root or alias nginx would use the default root. Here the alias is set, so the relative path is not used.
/srv/pics/
The file name is kept. Only the location prefix is swapped.
/srv/pics/cat.png
Right. alias REPLACES the matched part of the URI (/img/) with the alias path, so only cat.png is added.

q.q: You edited /etc/samba/smb.conf. Which command checks the file for mistakes and shows the settings Samba will actually use?
o: smbstatus
smbstatus lists current connections and locked files. It does not read the config for errors.
testparm
Right. testparm parses smb.conf, reports errors and prints the effective configuration after defaults are filled in.
smbclient -L localhost
This lists the shares a running server offers. It cannot tell you why the config is wrong.
net ads info
It shows details about the Active Directory domain. It does not check smb.conf syntax.

q.q: The Linux group "staff" must be able to connect to and write in the share [projects]. Everyone else must not be able to connect to it. Which settings do that?
o: read list = @staff  and  browseable = no
browseable = no only hides the share name in lists. Anyone who knows the name can still connect.
hosts allow = @staff  and  writable = yes
hosts allow takes host names or networks, not groups.
valid users = @staff  and  read only = no
Right. valid users limits who may connect (the @ means a Linux group). read only = no allows writing for those users.
admin users = @staff  and  guest ok = yes
admin users gives those users root-level rights on the share, which is too much, and guest ok opens it to everybody.

q.q: Samba is a standalone file server using the tdbsam backend. A Linux account alice already exists. Which command lets alice connect to shares from Windows?
o: smbpasswd -a alice
Right. -a adds the existing Unix user to Samba's own password database and sets an SMB password.
passwd alice (the Linux password)
This sets the Linux password. Samba (tdbsam) keeps separate password hashes and will not use it.
pdbedit -L -u alice
-L only LISTS the users that are already in the Samba database.
useradd -m -s /bin/bash alice
The account exists already, and useradd would not create a Samba entry anyway.

q.q: A Samba server with "security = ADS" and a correct realm and workgroup must become a member of the domain EXAMPLE.COM. Which command joins it (with the right permissions)?
o: kinit Administrator@EXAMPLE.COM
kinit only fetches a Kerberos ticket. It does not create a computer account.
winbindd -D
This starts the winbind daemon. It cannot join a domain by itself.
wbinfo -u
wbinfo -u lists domain users and only works AFTER the server has joined.
net ads join -U Administrator
Right. net ads join creates the computer account in Active Directory and stores the machine secret on the server.

q.q: A Samba domain member suddenly rejects all domain logins. You suspect the machine's secret with the domain controller is broken. Which command checks the trust?
o: wbinfo -u
-u lists domain users. It can work from cache and does not prove that the machine trust is valid.
testparm
testparm checks smb.conf, not the connection to the domain.
wbinfo -t
Right. -t checks the trust secret between this server and the domain. A failure means you may need to rejoin the domain.
smbstatus -b
smbstatus -b lists connected users with brief output. It does not test the trust.

q.q: A Linux client mounts //fs1/data in /etc/fstab with the CIFS type. The user name and password are in the fstab line, and anyone can read that file. What is the better practice?
o: Use credentials=/root/.smbcred in the options, with that file at mode 600
Right. The credentials file keeps the secret out of the world-readable fstab and only root can read it.
Replace the password with the NFS option "sec=sys" so no secret is needed
sec=sys is an NFS option. CIFS mounts do not use it.
Add the option "guest" and give everybody write rights on the share
That removes security instead of protecting the password.
Put the password in the options, but add "noauto"
noauto only stops mounting at boot. The password would still be readable.

q.q: From a Linux workstation you want to see which shares the file server fs1 offers, signed in as the user alice. Which command do you use?
o: showmount -e fs1 as user alice
showmount -e lists NFS exports, not Samba shares.
smbclient -L //fs1 -U alice
Right. -L lists the shares of a server, and -U sets the user name to log in with.
nmblookup -A fs1 -U alice
This asks for the NetBIOS name table of an address. It does not list shares.
smbstatus -S
-S lists shares in use on the LOCAL Samba server, not shares on a remote one.

q.q: Windows users sign in as "jsmith", but the matching Linux account is "john.smith". Which smb.conf setting maps one name to the other?
o: force user = john.smith in the share
force user makes EVERY connection to a share run as that one account, which would merge all users.
username map = /etc/samba/smbusers
Right. The map file has lines such as "john.smith = jsmith". Samba applies it at login time.
valid users = jsmith john.smith
valid users filters who may connect. It does not change the Linux account in use.
map to guest = Bad User in [global]
This turns unknown users into guest. It does not rename a valid user.

q.q: In smb.conf, the [printers] section contains "printable = yes" and "path = /var/spool/samba". What does printable = yes do?
o: It lets clients browse and delete other people's print jobs
Job control is set with other options and printable does not give it.
It makes the share read-only, so printing works only for the print admin
Printing needs writing to the spool path; printable does not make anything read-only.
It publishes the printer in Active Directory so clients can find it
Publishing to AD uses "published" settings and tools, not this flag.
It marks the share as a printer share that accepts spooled print jobs
Right. printable (or print ok) is what makes the section accept spooled print jobs. The path is the spool folder.

q.q: Which situation requires "samba-tool domain provision"?
o: You want Samba itself to act as an AD domain controller for a new domain
Right. provision builds the directory database, DNS and Kerberos setup for a new Samba AD domain.
You want a Samba server to join an existing Windows domain as a member
A member joins with net ads join. Provision would create a second domain instead.
You want a standalone file server with a few local users
Standalone servers need only smb.conf and smbpasswd.
You want to share a printer with Windows clients through CUPS
Printer shares need a [printers] section and CUPS, not a domain.

q.q: Share [data] has "read only = no" and alice is allowed to connect, but Windows says she cannot save files. On the server, the folder is owned by root with mode 755. What is the cause?
o: The share needs "guest ok = yes" before any normal user is allowed to write into it
Guest access would open the share to everyone and would not give write rights on the disk.
Samba ignores Linux file permissions whenever the share is set to read only = no
It does not ignore them. Samba checks the file system rights for every action.
Samba obeys Linux permissions, and alice has no write right on the folder
Right. Samba acts as the Linux user. Both the share settings and the Unix permissions must allow writing; the stricter one wins.
The server must also run nmbd before writes to the share can work
nmbd handles NetBIOS name service. It has no part in write permission.

q.q: Which TWO statements about Samba 4 as a domain MEMBER server (security = ADS) are true? (Choose two.)
o: Winbind maps domain users and groups to Linux accounts so file permissions can use them
Right. winbindd resolves domain names to UIDs and GIDs through the idmap settings.
Kerberos is used for authentication, so the server's clock must be close to the domain controller's time
Right. Kerberos tickets fail when the time difference is too large (5 minutes by default).
The member server stores all domain accounts in its own tdbsam
Accounts stay on the domain controller. The member server only maps them.
Domain users must also be added with smbpasswd -a on the member server
The password is checked by the domain controller, so smbpasswd -a is not needed.
The server must be the first domain controller
A member server is not a controller. It joins an existing domain.

q.q: You edited /etc/exports on the NFS server. Which command re-exports everything without restarting the NFS services?
o: exportfs -v
-v only lists the current exports with options. It changes nothing.
exportfs -ra
Right. -r re-reads /etc/exports and -a applies all entries, adding new ones and removing deleted ones.
showmount -a
It shows which clients have mounted shares, a status view only.
mount -a
mount -a mounts the entries of /etc/fstab. It does not read /etc/exports.

q.q: A client's root user creates a file on a mounted NFS export. On the server the file belongs to "nobody". Which export option causes this?
o: no_subtree_check
It turns off a check of whether a file is inside the exported subtree. It does not change owners.
sync
sync makes the server write changes to disk before replying. It does not map users.
insecure
insecure allows clients to connect from ports above 1023, which has nothing to do with user mapping.
root_squash
Right. root_squash (the default) maps requests from client root to the anonymous user, so a client root cannot act as server root.

q.q: A power cut hits the NFS server. Some files that clients had saved are damaged. Which export option setting gives the safest behavior against that kind of loss?
o: async
async replies before the data is on disk and is faster, but a crash can lose data that clients thought was saved.
ro
ro would make the export read-only. Nothing could be saved at all.
sync
Right. With sync the server replies "done" only after data is committed to stable storage.
all_squash
all_squash maps every user to the anonymous account. It does not change how data is written.

q.q: From a client, which command lists the exports offered by the server nfs1?
o: showmount -e nfs1
Right. -e prints the server's export list and the hosts that may use each export.
exportfs -v -a nfs1
exportfs works only on the LOCAL server and takes no host name.
nfsstat -c -o nfs
It prints client-side NFS statistics such as call counts. It does not list exports.
rpcinfo -s nfs1 | grep nfs
It lists registered RPC services but does not show which directories are exported.

q.q: A database server writes to an NFS mount. If the NFS server is briefly unreachable, writes must wait and continue instead of failing silently. Which mount option fits?
o: hard
Right. With hard, the client keeps retrying until the server answers, so applications never see a false success or lost write.
soft
soft gives up after the retries and returns an error, which can leave programs with partly written data.
ro
ro makes the mount read-only and the database cannot write.
nolock
nolock turns off file locking, which is risky for databases and has no effect on retries.

q.q: On a server that still uses TCP Wrappers for rpcbind, a client's address appears in neither /etc/hosts.allow nor /etc/hosts.deny. What happens?
o: Access is denied
Denial happens only when an entry in hosts.deny matches. Typical hardening adds "rpcbind: ALL" to hosts.deny.
Access is allowed
Right. The files are checked in order, hosts.allow first and then hosts.deny. With no match in either, access is granted.
Access is allowed only for root
TCP Wrappers do not look at user names for this service.
Access depends on the order of the lines in /etc/exports
/etc/exports is a separate control, and the wrappers do not read it.

q.q: Your firewall blocks everything except what you open. Clients use only NFSv4 to mount your server. Which is the minimum you must open?
o: TCP and UDP port 111 only
Port 111 is the portmapper used by NFSv3. NFSv4 clients talk straight to 2049.
TCP ports 137 to 139
These are NetBIOS ports used by older SMB file sharing, not NFS.
TCP port 2049
Right. NFSv4 works over a single well-known TCP port, 2049, and needs no rpcbind or mountd ports.
TCP port 445
Port 445 is SMB over TCP, which is Samba's port.

q.q: This line is in /etc/exports: "/srv/data 192.168.1.0/24 (rw,sync)", with a space before the bracket. What does it do?
o: It exports the folder only to 192.168.1.0/24 with rw and sync, as the line was meant to
Only if there is NO space between the host and the bracket.
It is rejected, and exportfs prints a syntax error about the space before the bracket
exportfs only prints a warning ('No host name given ... suggest *(...)') and still exports. It does not reject the line, which is why this typo is dangerous.
It exports the folder read-only to everybody and read-write to nobody
The brackets with rw apply to the world entry, so it is read-write.
It exports to EVERY host with rw, and 192.168.1.0/24 only gets the defaults
Right. The space ends the host entry. The options in brackets then apply to the world. A very common and dangerous typo.

q.q: A network printer with the MAC address 00:11:22:33:44:55 must always get 10.0.5.20 from the ISC DHCP server, while the dynamic range stays for other devices. What do you add to dhcpd.conf?
o: host printer1 { hardware ethernet 00:11:22:33:44:55; fixed-address 10.0.5.20; }
Right. A host block ties a client hardware address to a fixed address. Keep that address outside the dynamic range.
A second range statement "range 10.0.5.20 10.0.5.20;" for the printer's address
That gives the single address to the NEXT client that asks, not to one specific printer.
option routers 10.0.5.20; inside the subnet block
option routers hands out a default gateway address. It does not reserve an address for a device.
default-lease-time 0; in the subnet block
A lease time of 0 does not create reservations. Reservations come only from host declarations.

q.q: The DHCP server sits on VLAN 10. Clients on VLAN 20 get no lease, and a packet capture on the server shows no DISCOVER packets from VLAN 20. The router does not forward broadcasts. What is the standard fix?
o: Raise max-lease-time on the DHCP server so that clients keep their addresses longer
Lease time has no effect when the requests never arrive.
Add the line authoritative; to dhcpd.conf so the server answers requests from other networks
authoritative only makes the server send NAKs for wrong addresses. It does not help requests cross a router.
Install radvd on the VLAN 20 gateway so that clients get their addresses from router advertisements
radvd sends IPv6 router advertisements. It does not relay IPv4 DHCP.
Run dhcrelay on VLAN 20's gateway, pointing at the server, and add a VLAN 20 subnet block on the server
Right. The relay turns the broadcast into a unicast to the server. The server needs the subnet block to know which addresses to hand out.

q.q: You changed dhcpd.conf and want to check the syntax without starting the service. Which command?
o: dhcpd -T -lf /var/lib/dhcp/dhcpd.leases
-T (capital) tests the LEASE database file, not the config.
dhcpd -t -cf /etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf
Right. -t tests the configuration file and exits. -cf names the file to test.
dhcpd -q -cf /etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf
-q only keeps start-up quiet. It still starts the daemon.
dhclient -v
dhclient is the CLIENT program. It would ask for an address, not test the server's config.

q.q: IPv6 clients on a network must learn their default gateway and prefix. Which mechanism provides the default gateway for IPv6?
o: A DHCPv6 option named "routers" in dhcpd6.conf for each subnet
DHCPv6 has no default gateway option. That info comes from Router Advertisements.
A DHCPv4 relay agent running on the router's LAN port
DHCPv4 deals with IPv4. IPv6 uses other tools.
Router Advertisements (for example from radvd)
Right. The router announces itself, and clients build their gateway from it. DHCPv6 cannot hand out a gateway.
A static route written in /etc/hosts
/etc/hosts maps names to addresses. It cannot define routes.

q.q: A PAM stack has the line "auth required pam_unix.so". If this module fails, what happens?
o: PAM stops running the stack at once and returns failure to the calling program straight away
That is "requisite". required keeps running the other modules in the stack.
PAM ignores the failure if a later module in the stack succeeds
A later success does not cancel a failed required module.
The module is skipped as if it were not listed in the stack, and the rest decides
That is how an "optional" module behaves when it is not the only one.
It is recorded, the other modules still run, and the final result is failure
Right. required lets PAM continue with other modules so an attacker cannot tell which one failed, but the overall result is a fail.

q.q: In /etc/pam.d/sshd the first auth line is "auth sufficient pam_unix.so" and later lines are "auth required pam_deny.so". pam_unix succeeds and no earlier required module failed. What happens next?
o: PAM stops processing the auth stack and returns success
Right. A sufficient module that succeeds (and nothing required has failed) ends the stack with success, so pam_deny is never reached.
PAM goes on to pam_deny, which then fails the login for everyone
The stack ends early on success, so pam_deny never runs.
PAM asks for the password a second time
PAM does not repeat modules. Each one runs at most once per request.
PAM falls back to the account stack and ignores auth
The auth stack result comes first, and then account and session stacks run.

q.q: You must lock a user account for 10 minutes after 5 failed logins. Which PAM module (on a current RHEL-type system) provides this?
o: pam_limits
pam_limits sets resource limits such as open files or processes from limits.conf.
pam_faillock
Right. faillock counts failed attempts per user and locks the account for unlock_time seconds. It replaced pam_tally2.
pam_wheel
pam_wheel restricts who may use su, based on group.
pam_securetty
It restricts root logins to terminals listed in /etc/securetty, which is old and not about failure counts.

q.q: Only members of the group "wheel" should be able to use su to become root. Which line in /etc/pam.d/su does that?
o: account required pam_nologin.so file=/etc/nologin
pam_nologin blocks everybody except root when /etc/nologin exists. It is not group based.
session required pam_limits.so conf=/etc/security/limits.conf
It applies resource limits when a session starts, not group checks.
auth required pam_wheel.so use_uid
Right. pam_wheel makes su check for membership of wheel. use_uid uses the real user ID of the caller.
auth sufficient pam_rootok.so
pam_rootok lets root through without a password. It opens su for root only and is not a group filter.

q.q: /etc/nsswitch.conf contains "passwd: files sss". A user logs in who is not listed in /etc/passwd. Where does the system look next?
o: DNS, as the NSS name service
DNS is used by the hosts database, not passwd, unless configured.
/etc/shadow
shadow holds password hashes for users already in passwd. It does not list new accounts.
The login fails at once because only one source is allowed
A line can list many sources and they are tried in order.
SSSD, which can query LDAP or another remote directory
Right. Sources are tried left to right. files is local, and sss means System Security Services Daemon.

q.q: One entry in /etc/shadow is: alice:$6$x...:19800:0:90:7:14::. What does the number 90 mean?
o: The password must be changed at least every 90 days
Right. Fields are name, hash, last change, minimum age, maximum age (90), warning days, inactive days, expiry.
The account is locked for 90 days
Locking uses an exclamation mark in the hash field or a set expiry date.
The user gets a warning 90 days before the password expires
The warning period is the next field (7).
The password was last changed 90 days ago
The last-change field is 19800, a count of days since 1 January 1970.

q.q: In /etc/shadow, the hash field of the user bob begins with "!" (for example !$6$abc...). What does this mean?
o: bob has no password at all, so anyone can log in as bob without typing anything
An empty hash field means no password. The mark in front of a hash does the opposite.
bob's account has expired and cannot log in by any method until an admin extends it
Expiry is a separate field (number of days since 1970) and does not use the hash field.
Password logins for bob are locked, but key-based SSH may still work
Right. An exclamation mark in front of the hash disables password authentication (usermod -L does this). The account itself is not deleted.
bob's password hash uses the SHA-512 algorithm for storage
Algorithm is shown by the $6$ prefix. The exclamation mark in front is the lock.

q.q: After you edit /etc/sssd/sssd.conf, the sssd service will not start. The log says the file permissions check failed. What do you do?
o: chmod 777 /etc/sssd/sssd.conf so every service can read it
A world-writable config is exactly what sssd refuses.
chmod 600 /etc/sssd/sssd.conf, and make sure it is owned by root
Right. sssd refuses a config file that others can read, because it may hold bind passwords.
Move the file to /etc/ldap/ldap.conf, where the LDAP tools look
ldap.conf is read by the OpenLDAP client tools. sssd would find no config at all.
Add "selinux = off" in the [sssd] section of the same file
SELinux is not an sssd.conf setting.

q.q: In "ldapsearch -x -H ldap://ldap.example.com -b dc=example,dc=com (uid=alice)", what does -x do?
o: It uses StartTLS before sending the query to the server
StartTLS is switched on with -Z or -ZZ.
It makes the output leave out attributes that have no value
-x has no effect on output.
It sets the search base to the root of the server's tree
The base is set with -b, as seen in the command.
It uses simple authentication (or anonymous) instead of SASL
Right. With -x, ldapsearch binds with a DN and password, or without credentials when no -D is given.

q.q: Which command changes the password of the LDAP entry uid=alice,ou=People,dc=example,dc=com, asking for a new password to enter?
o: ldapadd -x -D "cn=admin,dc=example,dc=com" -W -S "uid=alice,ou=People,dc=example,dc=com" -f alice.ldif
ldapadd adds entries from LDIF. It has no -S option.
ldappasswd -x -D "cn=admin,dc=example,dc=com" -W -S "uid=alice,ou=People,dc=example,dc=com"
Right. ldappasswd uses the LDAP password modify operation. -S prompts for the new password.
ldapwhoami -x -D "cn=admin,dc=example,dc=com" -W -S "uid=alice,ou=People,dc=example,dc=com" -v
ldapwhoami reports who you are bound as and has no -S option. It changes nothing.
passwd alice (the Linux password)
passwd changes the local /etc/shadow password and does not touch the LDAP directory.

q.q: In an LDIF file for ldapmodify, one entry gets two changes: replace the mail attribute and then add a telephoneNumber. What separates the two changes?
o: A blank line between the two changes of the entry
A blank line ends the whole entry and starts a new one with a new dn.
A line starting with # and a space, as a comment
That is a comment line and does not end any change.
A line containing only a hyphen (-)
Right. Inside one entry, a single "-" ends one change so the next change can follow.
A line with "---" and a dn
A new dn would start a different entry. The separator is just one hyphen.

q.q: Which LDAP filter returns entries of class posixAccount whose uid is alice OR bob?
o: (&(objectClass=posixAccount)(|(uid=alice)(uid=bob)))
Right. & means AND, | means OR. Operators come first in prefix notation, with each test in its own brackets.
(objectClass=posixAccount)&(uid=alice|bob)
This is not valid LDAP syntax. Operators must be inside the brackets and written first.
(&(objectClass=posixAccount)(&(uid=alice)(uid=bob))(uid=*))
An entry cannot have uid equal to both values at once, so nothing would match.
(|(objectClass=posixAccount)(uid=alice)(uid=bob)(uid=*))
This matches EVERY posixAccount, plus alice and bob, because OR is at the top.

q.q: Which command deletes the entry uid=bob,ou=People,dc=example,dc=com from the directory, after you have bound as the admin DN?
o: ldapdelete -x -D "cn=admin,dc=example,dc=com" -W "uid=bob,ou=People,dc=example,dc=com"
Right. ldapdelete takes the DN of each entry to remove. Without -r it refuses to delete an entry that has children.
ldapsearch -x -D "cn=admin,dc=example,dc=com" -W -b "uid=bob,ou=People,dc=example,dc=com" --delete
ldapsearch only reads. It has no delete option.
slapcat -b "uid=bob,ou=People,dc=example,dc=com" -d
slapcat dumps the database to LDIF and does not remove entries.
ldapmodify -x -D "cn=admin,dc=example,dc=com" -W "uid=bob,ou=People,dc=example,dc=com"
ldapmodify needs LDIF input, usually with "changetype: delete". Giving only the DN is not enough.

q.q: A modern OpenLDAP slapd stores its configuration under /etc/ldap/slapd.d (cn=config). What is the supported way to change an access rule while slapd runs?
o: Edit the .ldif files in slapd.d with a text editor and then restart slapd
Hand edits break the checksum in each file, and slapd may refuse to read them.
Run slapindex on the database and then restart slapd to apply the new rule
slapindex rebuilds indexes only. It does not change access rules.
ldapmodify -Y EXTERNAL -H ldapi:/// with an LDIF change to cn=config
Right. The ldapi socket with EXTERNAL authentication lets the local root user edit the live configuration.
Copy the rule into /etc/ldap/ldap.conf and restart slapd
ldap.conf configures LDAP CLIENTS, not the server.

q.q: In the DN uid=alice,ou=People,dc=example,dc=com, which part is the RDN (relative distinguished name) of the entry?
o: ou=People
This is the parent entry (an organizational unit that holds users).
uid=alice
Right. The RDN is the leftmost part. It identifies the entry among its siblings under the parent.
dc=example,dc=com
It is the base of the directory tree (the suffix), not part of the RDN.
uid=alice,ou=People
This is the DN minus the suffix. The RDN is only the leftmost component.

q.q: Adding an entry with objectClass inetOrgPerson fails with "object class 'inetOrgPerson' requires attribute 'sn'". What is wrong?
o: The attribute sn is MAY, and the server dislikes empty values for every attribute
The message says "requires", so sn is MUST. It is not a rule about empty values.
slapd must be restarted before it loads the installed schema, which has not happened
Schemas that are already installed are used at once. The error comes from the entry itself.
The base DN of the directory does not exist on this server yet
A missing parent gives a different error ("no such object").
The entry lacks an attribute that the object class marks as MUST
Right. The schema lists required (MUST) and optional (MAY) attributes. inetOrgPerson, through person, requires sn and cn.

q.q: Which object class supplies the attributes uidNumber and homeDirectory that Linux needs for a user account stored in LDAP?
o: inetOrgPerson
It holds personal data such as mail and displayName. It has no uidNumber.
posixAccount
Right. posixAccount (from the nis schema) carries uid, uidNumber, gidNumber and homeDirectory for Unix accounts.
organizationalUnit
It creates a container like ou=People. It does not describe a user.
posixGroup
posixGroup describes groups with gidNumber and memberUid. It has no homeDirectory.

q.q: You want an offline backup of an OpenLDAP database to a text file, directly from the database files. Which tool?
o: slapcat
Right. slapcat reads the database back end directly and writes LDIF, even when slapd is not running.
slapadd
slapadd does the reverse: it loads LDIF INTO the database.
slapindex
slapindex rebuilds the indexes of a database. It writes no LDIF.
ldappasswd
ldappasswd changes one password over the network. It does not dump anything.

q.q: You ran "slapadd -l data.ldif" as root on a stopped server. Now slapd (running as the user openldap) cannot open the database. What fixes it?
o: Rebuild the schema with slapcat and load it again
slapcat only exports data. The permission problem remains.
Set olcReadOnly: TRUE on the database in cn=config
A read-only database still needs the daemon to be able to open the files.
Add -u root to the slapd start options so it can open the files
Running the daemon as root defeats the purpose of a limited user and is not the fix.
chown -R openldap:openldap on the database directory
Right. slapadd as root creates files owned by root. The daemon user needs to own them.

q.q: You added "olcDbIndex: mail eq" to a database that already holds many entries. Searches on mail are still slow. Which step builds the new index for the existing entries?
o: Run ldapsearch with the new mail filter to warm the index
ldapsearch only reads the directory. It does not build an index for entries that already exist.
Run ldapsearch with -z 0 to trigger indexing
-z limits the number of entries returned and does not index anything.
Stop slapd, run slapindex, then start slapd again
Right. A new index only covers entries added or changed AFTER the setting. slapindex rebuilds it for the current data.
Restart the client with sss_cache -E
sss_cache clears the SSSD client cache and does not touch the server index.

q.q: An access rule reads: "olcAccess: {0}to attrs=userPassword by self write by anonymous auth by * none". What does it do?
o: Everyone can read every user's password hash, but only the owner may change it, and nobody else may
"by * none" refuses all other access, including reading.
Anonymous users may write any password, while all other users have no access at all to the entry
anonymous gets auth only, which is a login check and not a write.
It applies to every attribute of every entry in the directory, not only passwords
The "to attrs=userPassword" part limits the rule to that single attribute.
Users change their own password, anonymous clients can only log in, nobody else can read it
Right. self write allows own password changes. anonymous auth allows only authentication, and * none refuses everything else.

q.q: The first access rule of a database is "to * by * read", and the second is "to attrs=userPassword by * none". Users can still read password hashes. Why?
o: olcAccess rules are all checked, and the most permissive one wins, so the broad rule just grants more
OpenLDAP uses the FIRST rule that matches the target, not a vote.
The first matching "to" clause wins, so the broad rule hides the specific one
Right. Order matters. Put specific rules first and the general rule last.
by * none cannot be used for the userPassword attribute at all, so the server skips it
It is a normal rule. The problem is that it comes second.
Rules are checked from the highest to the lowest number in braces
The lowest number ({0}) is checked first.

q.q: An LDIF file has a long description attribute that must continue on the next line. How is the continuation written?
o: The first line ends with a backslash
LDIF does not use a backslash for continuation.
The next line starts with a plus sign
A plus sign is used in a multi-part RDN, not for continuation.
The next line starts with a single space
Right. In LDIF a line that begins with one space continues the previous line, and that space is not part of the value.
A blank line is placed between the two parts
A blank line ends the whole entry.

q.q: You want a short list of only the Postfix settings that differ from the built-in defaults, to read in a ticket. Which command prints it?
o: postconf -n
Right. -n shows only parameters that were changed in main.cf. It is a fast way to review a Postfix setup.
postconf -d
-d prints the DEFAULT values, the opposite of what you want.
postfix check
check tests directory and file permissions. It prints nothing about your settings.
postqueue -p
-p prints the mail queue, not the configuration.

q.q: You edited /etc/aliases to forward the name "helpdesk" to three people. Postfix still sends mail to the old address. Which command updates the lookup table used by Postfix?
o: postmap /etc/aliases
postmap is for ordinary lookup tables. Aliases use postalias, which newaliases runs for you.
postconf -e alias_maps=
It would change the setting that names the table, not rebuild the data.
newaliases
Right. It rebuilds the indexed aliases database (aliases.db) from the text file.
postsuper -r ALL
postsuper -r puts queued mail back in the queue. It does not touch aliases.

q.q: Mail to a partner has been waiting in the Postfix queue since the partner's server was down. It is back up now. Which command asks Postfix to try delivering every queued message right away?
o: postqueue -f
Right. -f flushes the queue, so Postfix retries all deferred mail at once.
postqueue -p
-p only prints the queue contents.
postsuper -d ALL
-d ALL DELETES all queued mail. The messages would be lost.
postcat -q ABC123
postcat prints the content of one queued message and does not deliver it.

q.q: A spam source relays mail through your Postfix server to outside recipients without logging in. The server is in a lab and you check main.cf. Which setting is the most likely cause?
o: mydestination = $myhostname
This only lists domains that are delivered locally. It does not open relaying.
smtpd_tls_security_level = may
It makes TLS optional on the SMTP server. It has no effect on who can relay.
message_size_limit = 0
A value of 0 means no size limit. That is a different risk and not open relaying.
mynetworks = 0.0.0.0/0
Right. It tells Postfix that every address on the Internet is "local", so it relays mail for them.

q.q: Which main.cf setting makes Postfix offer STARTTLS to clients that connect to its SMTP server, while still accepting clients that do not use encryption?
o: smtpd_tls_security_level = encrypt
encrypt requires TLS from every client. Plain connections would be refused.
smtpd_tls_security_level = may
Right. may means opportunistic TLS for incoming connections. Clients that do not ask for TLS can still send mail.
smtp_tls_security_level = may
The setting without the "d" applies when Postfix is the CLIENT, sending mail out.
smtpd_use_tls = no
This turns TLS off on the SMTP server. It is the opposite of what is wanted.

q.q: In a lab, you test your own Postfix server by hand with telnet to port 25. After you type the message headers and body, how do you tell SMTP the message is finished?
o: Press Ctrl+D to close the input and finish the message
Ctrl+D closes the input to telnet but does not complete the SMTP transaction.
Type QUIT before the body
QUIT ends the session, so the body would never be sent.
Send a line that contains only a single period
Right. A line with just "." ends the DATA part. The server then queues the message.
Send two blank lines after the body of the message to finish
A blank line separates headers from the body. Two blank lines do not end the DATA.

q.q: /var/log/mail.log shows: "to=<joe@example.net>, relay=mx.example.net[198.51.100.9]:25, status=deferred (connect to mx.example.net[198.51.100.9]:25: Connection timed out)". What does it mean?
o: Delivery failed for now. Postfix keeps the message and tries again later
Right. deferred is a temporary failure, such as a timeout or a busy remote server. Postfix retries until the queue lifetime ends.
Delivery is complete and the remote server accepted the mail
That would be status=sent.
The remote server said the user does not exist, and the sender got a bounce
An unknown user gives a permanent 5xx and status=bounced.
Postfix rejected the mail because of a policy rule
A rejection on your side would show "reject" in the log and the SMTP error to the sender.

q.q: sendmail is the mail server on an older host. You need to change its configuration. What is the usual workflow?
o: Edit /etc/postfix/main.cf, then run postfix reload to apply the change
Those are Postfix files and commands.
Edit sendmail.mc, run m4 to build sendmail.cf, then restart sendmail
Right. sendmail.cf is hard to edit, so admins edit the short macro file and generate the real config from it.
Edit /etc/exim4/exim4.conf, then run exim -bt to rebuild it
Those belong to Exim, a different mail server.
Edit sendmail.cf by hand and then run newaliases to apply it
You can edit sendmail.cf, but it is not the usual way, and newaliases only rebuilds the aliases database.

q.q: You added a line to /etc/postfix/virtual to map sales@example.com to two mailboxes, and virtual_alias_maps points to hash:/etc/postfix/virtual. Mail is still not redirected. What is missing?
o: newaliases to rebuild the aliases database
That rebuilds /etc/aliases and not the virtual table.
postsuper -r ALL
It requeues messages and does not change lookup tables.
A new MX record for example.com in the DNS zone
An MX record controls where outside servers send mail. The mapping happens inside Postfix after the mail has arrived.
postmap /etc/postfix/virtual to build the indexed .db file (then reload)
Right. A hash: table is read from the .db file, so the text file must be converted after each edit.

q.q: A Sieve script uses fileinto "Lists" and the mail server refuses to compile it with "unknown command fileinto". What do you add at the top?
o: include "fileinto" :personal;
include loads another script, not an extension.
use fileinto from sieve;
This is not Sieve syntax.
import ["fileinto"]; (loads it)
Sieve has no import command.
require ["fileinto"];
Right. Sieve extensions must be declared with require before use. fileinto is an extension, not part of the base language.

q.q: Which Sieve rule moves mail from the sender list@example.org into the folder Lists? (The fileinto extension is already required.)
o: if header "from" == "list@example.org" { fileinto "Lists"; }
Sieve has no == operator. Tests use match types such as :is and :contains.
if address :is "from" "list@example.org" { fileinto "Lists"; }
Right. address :is tests the address part of a header for an exact match.
if size :is "from" "list@example.org" { fileinto "Lists"; stop; }
size tests message length and not sender.
fileinto "Lists" where from = "list@example.org" and size > 1;
Sieve has no where clause. Conditions use if.

q.q: A user wants all messages larger than 10 MB to be refused silently, with no bounce message to the sender. Which Sieve is right?
o: if size :larger 10M { reject "too big"; }
:larger is not a Sieve test, and reject sends a bounce.
if size :under 10M { discard; }
:under matches SMALL messages, so normal mail would be thrown away.
if size :over 10M { discard; }
Right. size :over compares the message size. discard drops the message without telling the sender.
if header :over "size" "10M" { stop; }
header tests text of a header and has no :over match type. stop ends processing but does not delete.

q.q: In a procmail recipe file, which line starts a new recipe?
o: Right. Every recipe begins with :0 (optionally followed by flags and a lock file name), then the condition lines starting with * and the action line.
* ^Subject:.*invoice
This is a condition line. It follows the :0 line.
INCLUDERC=/etc/procmailrc
This variable assignment includes another file.
| /usr/bin/spamassassin
A line starting with | is an ACTION that pipes the message to a program. It is also part of an existing recipe.

q.q: Users should upload and edit their Sieve scripts from their mail client without shell access. Which protocol and default port does this?
o: ManageSieve on TCP 4190
Right. ManageSieve is a protocol made to manage Sieve scripts remotely. Dovecot's Pigeonhole plugin provides it.
IMAP on TCP 993
IMAPS delivers mail to clients. Scripts are not uploaded through it.
SMTP submission on TCP 587
Submission is for sending mail, not for filter scripts.
POP3 on TCP 110
POP3 downloads mail. It has no script commands.

q.q: Which Dovecot command prints only the settings that differ from the defaults, so you can review a mailbox server's configuration?
o: doveadm who
It lists logged-in users and connections, and not the configuration.
doveconf -n
Right. -n prints only the settings that differ from the built-in defaults, which keeps the output short.
dovecot --build-options
This prints how the binary was built, not the live settings.
doveadm reload
It tells the running Dovecot to re-read its configuration. It prints nothing about it.

q.q: The Dovecot service must offer only IMAP and no POP3. Which setting in dovecot.conf does that?
o: mail_plugins = imap
mail_plugins loads extra code into mail processing. It is not the switch for protocols.
disable_plaintext_auth = yes
It forbids passwords on unencrypted connections for all protocols. POP3 stays enabled.
login_trusted_networks = 0.0.0.0/0
It lists networks that may pass client IP info to Dovecot. It does not stop protocols.
protocols = imap
Right. The protocols setting lists which mail protocols Dovecot starts listeners for.

q.q: Which Dovecot line correctly points to the server certificate file for TLS (Dovecot 2.x)?
o: ssl_cert = /etc/dovecot/certs/mail.pem
Without the < Dovecot reads the path text as a certificate and fails to start TLS.
ssl_cert_file = /etc/dovecot/certs/mail.pem
That is not a Dovecot 2.x setting name.
ssl_cert = </etc/dovecot/certs/mail.pem
Right. The leading < tells Dovecot to read the VALUE from the named file. Without it, Dovecot treats the text as the certificate itself.
ssl_ca = </etc/dovecot/certs/mail.pem
ssl_ca names trusted CA certificates for checking client certificates, not the server's own.

q.q: A phone app is set to "IMAP, port 993, STARTTLS" and fails with "connection closed". The Dovecot log shows "imap-login: Disconnected: Aborted login (no auth attempts)", and doveconf shows an inet_listener imaps with port = 993 and ssl = yes. What is wrong?
o: Port 993 expects TLS from the very first byte, so the app must use SSL/TLS (implicit), or use port 143 with STARTTLS
Right. The imaps listener speaks TLS at once, so a client that starts in plain text and sends STARTTLS is dropped.
Dovecot must set ssl = no on port 993 so that STARTTLS can work
Turning TLS off would not fix a mismatch and would put passwords in clear text.
The app must use port 995 for IMAP over TLS
995 is POP3 over TLS. IMAP over TLS uses 993.
The imap-login service must listen on port 587 for STARTTLS
587 is the mail submission port. STARTTLS for IMAP uses port 143.

q.q: You want Dovecot to refuse password logins until the connection is protected by TLS. Which setting does it?
o: auth_verbose = yes
It only writes more details about authentication to the log.
disable_plaintext_auth = yes
Right. With TLS not active, Dovecot will not accept plain passwords, so clients must use STARTTLS or implicit TLS first.
ssl = no
It turns TLS off, which makes things worse.
mail_location = maildir:~/Maildir
It tells Dovecot where mail is stored and has nothing to do with login rules.

q.q: A Linux gateway between two lab networks does not pass packets between its two interfaces. Which sysctl setting turns on IPv4 routing and is made permanent in /etc/sysctl.conf (or a file in /etc/sysctl.d)?
o: net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1
rp_filter checks that replies would leave by the same interface. It is anti-spoofing and does not enable routing.
net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_all = 1
It makes the host ignore ping requests, which has nothing to do with forwarding.
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
Right. This allows the kernel to forward packets that are not addressed to the machine itself.
net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6 = 1
It switches IPv6 off. IPv4 forwarding stays off.

q.q: Your router connects a private LAN to the Internet through eth0 (the public side). Which rule gives the LAN access using the router's public address?
o: iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE
-o (output interface) is not allowed in PREROUTING, because the route is not chosen yet.
iptables -A FORWARD -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE
MASQUERADE works only in the nat table, so this rule is rejected.
iptables -t nat -A INPUT -i eth0 -j SNAT
The nat table has no INPUT chain in the usual setup, and SNAT needs a --to-source address.
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE
Right. NAT for outgoing traffic is done in the nat table POSTROUTING chain. MASQUERADE uses the address of the outgoing interface.

q.q: You must send traffic arriving on the router's eth0, TCP port 8080, to the internal web server 192.168.1.20 port 80. Which nat rule does the address change?
o: iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -i eth0 -p tcp --dport 8080 -j DNAT --to-destination 192.168.1.20:80
DNAT cannot be used in POSTROUTING, and -i is not allowed there either.
iptables -A INPUT -i eth0 -p tcp --dport 8080 -j REDIRECT --to-ports 80
REDIRECT sends traffic to a port on the router itself, not to another host, and it belongs in the nat table.
