iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -i eth0 -p tcp --dport 8080 -j DNAT --to-destination 192.168.1.20:80
Right. DNAT rewrites the destination before routing. You also need a FORWARD rule that allows the traffic.
iptables -t nat -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 8080 -j MASQUERADE --to-ports 80
The OUTPUT chain handles packets made by the router itself, and MASQUERADE would not change the destination.

q.q: The FORWARD chain policy is DROP. LAN clients send requests out through the router, but replies never come back. Which rule is missing?
o: iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
The INPUT chain is only for packets addressed to the router itself. Replies to LAN clients travel through FORWARD.
iptables -A FORWARD -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
Right. It accepts packets that belong to connections the router already allowed, which includes the replies.
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT
The nat table only sees the first packet of a connection, and it is for address rewriting, not for filtering.
iptables -P FORWARD ACCEPT, which allows all forwarded traffic
It would fix the problem, but it removes all filtering. The question asks for the missing rule, not for opening everything.

q.q: A server's INPUT chain begins with "-A INPUT -j DROP" and a later rule "-A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT". SSH is blocked. Which command puts the allow rule where it will work?
o: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT # as the last rule
-A appends at the END, after the DROP rule, so it is never reached.
iptables -D INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT # remove it
-D deletes the rule.
iptables -Z INPUT
-Z resets packet counters. It does not change order.
iptables -I INPUT 1 -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
Right. -I INPUT 1 inserts the rule at position 1, before the DROP rule. Rules are checked in order and the first match wins.

q.q: You have a working set of IPv4 rules. Which command writes them out in a format that iptables-restore can load again after a reboot?
o: iptables-save
Right. It prints all tables and chains in restore format. Redirect the output into the file that your distribution loads at boot.
iptables -L -n -v
This is a human-friendly listing. It cannot be loaded back with iptables-restore.
iptables-restore
It reads rules from input and loads them. It does not write anything out.
iptables -Z
It zeroes counters and nothing is saved.

q.q: The IPv4 firewall on a dual-stack server blocks port 23. A scan from another host still finds port 23 open over IPv6. What is the reason?
o: The scan used UDP, which iptables does not cover on either IP version
iptables handles TCP and UDP alike.
iptables rules apply only to IPv4, so ip6tables needs its own rules
Right. The two stacks have separate rule sets. Many admins forget the IPv6 side.
The kernel ignores rules for ports below 1024
Port numbers do not make rules optional.
ip_forward must be set to 2 for IPv6
It is a different setting (net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding), and values other than 0 or 1 are not used for this.

q.q: vsftpd should refuse logins by the user "anonymous" and "ftp". Which setting in vsftpd.conf does that?
o: anonymous_enable=NO
Right. With this, only real local users (if local_enable=YES) can log in.
local_enable=NO (local users)
This would stop local accounts, the normal users, and not anonymous logins.
no_anon_password=NO for anonymous
It controls whether anonymous users are asked for a password, not whether they may log in.
ftpd_banner=Closed (greeting)
The banner only changes the greeting text.

q.q: vsftpd is set with chroot_local_user=YES. Users log in and get "500 OOPS: vsftpd: refusing to run with writable root inside chroot()". What is the clean fix?
o: Set chroot_local_user=NO for all users, so nobody is kept in a jail
It removes the jail for everyone, which is less secure than the problem.
Run vsftpd as root using the setting run_as_root=YES to skip the check
There is no such setting, and running as root would make things worse.
Make the user's root folder read-only and put uploads in a writable subfolder
Right. vsftpd refuses a writable chroot root because of a security risk. The safest option is a read-only root with a writable subfolder.
Enable passive mode with pasv_enable=YES so the check is skipped
Passive mode controls data connections. It does not change the chroot check.

q.q: FTP users on the Internet log in through your firewall, but a directory listing hangs. Port 21 is open. They use passive mode. Which firewall change is also needed?
o: Allow TCP port 20 from the server to the client, because that is how passive mode connects
Port 20 is the source port of the server in ACTIVE mode, not passive.
Allow UDP port 21 for the data connection from the server back to the client
FTP control uses TCP.
Allow TCP port 22 for the file listing
Port 22 is SSH. SFTP uses it, not FTP.
Allow the passive port range set by pasv_min_port and pasv_max_port
Right. In passive mode the CLIENT opens the data connection to a port chosen by the server from that range.

q.q: Anonymous uploads fail, even though anon_upload_enable=YES is set. Which other setting is required in vsftpd.conf?
o: anon_world_readable_only=NO
It affects who may download. It does not allow uploads.
local_umask=000
It sets permissions on files uploaded by LOCAL users, not by anonymous users.
listen_ipv6=YES
It makes vsftpd listen on IPv6 and has no effect on uploads.
write_enable=YES
Right. vsftpd allows any change to the file system only if write_enable is on. anon_upload_enable alone is not enough.

q.q: With Pure-FTPd virtual users, you add a user with "pure-pw useradd bob -u ftpuser -d /srv/ftp/bob". The user still cannot log in. Which step is missing?
o: pure-pw show bob
show only displays the user's details.
pure-pw mkdb
Right. Pure-FTPd reads a compiled database. mkdb builds it from the password file after every change.
vsftpd -t
vsftpd is a different program from Pure-FTPd.
proftpd --configtest
ProFTPd is another FTP server, so this checks a different config.

q.q: A scan says root can still log in over SSH. sshd_config has "PermitRootLogin no" on line 33, but "sshd -T | grep permitrootlogin" prints "permitrootlogin yes". Line 12 is "Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf", and that folder holds 50-cloud.conf with "PermitRootLogin yes". Why does root still get in?
o: The last value wins, so line 33 applies and the scan result is wrong
sshd -T prints the values sshd really uses. For this keyword the first value wins, not the last.
PermitRootLogin only counts when UsePAM is set to no
The two settings are independent. UsePAM does not switch PermitRootLogin on or off.
sshd uses the FIRST value it reads for a keyword, and the included file is read before line 33, so remove or edit the drop-in
Right. For most keywords the first value wins. The Include at line 12 pulls in 50-cloud.conf before line 33, so its yes is used.
A global PermitRootLogin is ignored unless it is repeated in a Match block
Global settings work without a Match block. The problem is the order of the files.

q.q: You are logged in over SSH to a remote lab server and need to change sshd_config. Which method keeps you from locking yourself out?
o: Run sshd -t, reload sshd, keep your session open and test a new login in a second window
Right. A reload does not drop existing sessions, and the open session lets you undo a mistake.
Edit the file, restart sshd and then log out to check that the change works
If the new config is wrong, you cannot log in again and have no session to fix it.
Edit the file and reboot the server so that you know the config is applied
A reboot drops your session and takes the server offline.
Change the port, close port 22 in the firewall first, and then test the new port
Closing the old port first removes your way back if the new one fails.

q.q: Alice ran "cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys" on her laptop. She then tries to log in to server1 with her key and is still asked for a password. Which step is missing?
o: The public key must be added to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on server1 (ssh-copy-id alice@server1 does this)
Right. The server reads authorized_keys in the home folder of the account you log in as ON THE SERVER. Adding the key on the laptop changes nothing there.
The private key must be copied to ~/.ssh on server1
A private key must never leave the machine it was made on. The server needs only the public half.
ssh-add must be run on server1 to load the key
ssh-add feeds keys to an agent on the machine where you run it. It does not install keys on a server.
The key must be added to known_hosts on the laptop
known_hosts stores SERVER host keys so you can spot a changed server. It does not hold your login key.

q.q: Key login does not work. /var/log/auth.log says: "Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes for directory /home/alice". What is the cause?
o: The public key file is too short to be accepted as a valid key, so the server skips the file
A short key would show a different error, such as an invalid key format.
PasswordAuthentication is enabled, which blocks key logins for every user on the server
Enabling passwords does not cause this message.
The home folder is writable by group or others, so StrictModes refuses the keys
Right. With StrictModes yes, sshd checks that the home, .ssh and authorized_keys cannot be changed by others. Fix with chmod go-w.
The client is using the wrong port to reach the server
A wrong port would give "connection refused" before any key check.

q.q: Only members of the Linux group "sshusers" may log in over SSH. Which sshd_config line does that?
o: DenyGroups sshusers
It would block exactly the people you want to allow.
AllowGroups sshusers
Right. When AllowGroups is set, only users in a listed group are allowed. Everyone else is refused.
AllowUsers @sshusers
AllowUsers takes user names (with optional host patterns). It does not accept a leading @ for groups.
PermitUserEnvironment sshusers
It controls whether users may set environment variables through ssh, and takes yes or no.

q.q: Every admin now logs in with keys. Which sshd_config setting removes password guessing as an attack path, once you have tested that key login works?
o: PubkeyAuthentication no
It would turn keys off, the opposite of the plan.
MaxAuthTries 100 attempts
It allows more tries per connection, which helps the attacker.
LoginGraceTime 0 seconds
It removes the time limit for logging in and invites trouble.
PasswordAuthentication no
Right. The server then accepts only keys (and other non-password methods). Brute-force password attempts cannot succeed.

q.q: You run "eval $(ssh-agent)" and then "ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519" and type the key's passphrase once. What is the benefit?
o: The private key is copied to every server you connect to, so it is always available there
Keys never leave your machine. Only a signature is sent.
The passphrase is stored in clear text in ~/.ssh/config for later use
The agent does not write the passphrase to disk.
The key becomes usable by every user who is logged in on the machine
The agent is reachable only through your own socket.
Later SSH logins use the unlocked key held by the agent, with no passphrase prompt
Right. The agent keeps the unlocked key in memory for this login session only.

q.q: From your laptop you must reach the internal web server intranet.example.com:80 through the bastion host b1, so that http://localhost:8080 shows the intranet page. Which command?
o: ssh -R 8080:intranet.example.com:80 alice@b1
-R opens a port on the REMOTE side (b1) and forwards it back to you.
ssh -L 8080:intranet.example.com:80 alice@b1
Right. -L opens a local port and forwards it through b1 to the target host and port.
ssh -D 8080 alice@b1
-D builds a SOCKS proxy on localhost:8080. A browser would need proxy settings, and no fixed target is used.
ssh -X alice@b1
-X forwards graphical X11 programs and does not tunnel ports.

q.q: You want password login for the user "backup" only, from the internal network, while the global setting stays PasswordAuthentication no. What do you use?
o: A Match User backup Address 10.0.0.0/8 block at the END of sshd_config with PasswordAuthentication yes
Right. A Match block overrides settings for the conditions that follow, and it applies until the next Match line or the end of the file.
A PasswordAuthentication yes line placed before the global one at the top of the file
For global lines sshd uses the FIRST value it finds, so this would enable passwords for every user, not only backup. Only a Match block limits the change to one user.
Two sshd services that listen on the same port with different settings
Two daemons cannot share a port, and it would not solve the problem.
AllowUsers backup in the global part of sshd_config, which also turns passwords on
AllowUsers only decides who may log in. It does not turn passwords on.

q.q: After a server was rebuilt, ssh shows "WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED". You checked with the server's owner that the rebuild is real. What should you do?
o: Set StrictHostKeyChecking no in the global ssh config for all hosts
It turns off an important protection against man-in-the-middle attacks for every host.
Delete the whole ~/.ssh directory so that all stored keys are removed
That would also remove your private keys.
Run ssh-keygen -R server1, then connect again and check the new fingerprint
Right. Removing the stale entry is safe only after you have confirmed that the change is legitimate.
Ignore the warning because the connection is encrypted anyway, so nothing can go wrong
Encryption does not help if you talk to a different machine.

q.q: You have written permission to scan your own lab server 192.0.2.10. Which command checks ALL 65535 TCP ports for open services?
o: -sn is a ping scan that finds live hosts and skips port scanning.
Right. -p- means every port from 1 to 65535. By default nmap does a TCP scan (SYN scan when run as root).
-F is a fast scan of only the most common 100 ports.
-sU scans UDP, and only the top 1000 UDP ports by default.

q.q: A web app will not start and logs "bind: Address already in use" for port 8080. Which command, run as root on the server, shows which program is already listening on that port?
o: ss -tn | grep :8080
Without -l it lists connections that already exist, not listening sockets, and without -p it never names the program.
ss -s | grep 8080
-s prints only summary counts of sockets. No ports appear in it.
netstat -rn | grep 8080
-r shows the routing table. A port number does not appear in it.
ss -tlnp | grep :8080
Right. t = TCP, l = listening only, n = numbers, p = process. As root it shows the program name and PID that holds the port.

q.q: In a fail2ban jail, "maxretry = 5", "findtime = 10m" and "bantime = 1h". When is an IP address banned?
o: After 5 failures within 10 minutes, and then it stays banned for 1 hour
Right. findtime is the window in which the failures must happen, and bantime is how long the ban lasts.
After 5 failures in total, no matter how long ago, and the ban lasts 10 minutes
Failures must fall in the findtime window, and 10 minutes is not the ban time.
After 10 failures within 5 minutes, and the ban then lasts for 1 hour in total
The numbers are swapped. maxretry is 5 and findtime is 10 minutes.
After 5 failures within 1 hour, and then it stays banned for 10 minutes
The values for findtime and bantime are swapped.

q.q: A user typed a wrong password too often and fail2ban banned the IP 192.0.2.7 in the sshd jail. How do you remove just that ban?
o: iptables -F to clear the firewall
It flushes ALL firewall rules, including every other protection.
fail2ban-client stop, then start it again
It stops the whole service, which removes every ban and the protection.
fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip 192.0.2.7
Right. It removes the ban for one address in one jail and leaves other bans in place.
fail2ban-client reload --unban-all-sshd
This is not a valid fail2ban command.

q.q: With written permission, you test your own lab mail server mx1 from another lab host. You only need to know whether TCP port 25 accepts a connection, without sending any mail. Which command does that?
o: nc -l mx1 25
-l makes nc LISTEN on a port instead of connecting. It would not test mx1 at all.
nc -zv mx1 25
Right. -z checks the port without sending data and -v reports the result. A success line such as 'Connection to mx1 25 port [tcp/smtp] succeeded!' means the port is reachable.
traceroute -p 25 mx1
traceroute -p sets the destination port of its probe packets to map the route. It does not report whether a service accepts a connection.
ping -p 25 mx1
-p gives a byte pattern to fill the ICMP packet. It does not choose a TCP port, and ping cannot test one.

q.q: The lab server's auth log shows hundreds of failed SSH logins from one address. Which tool reads logs like this and bans the address automatically with a firewall rule?
o: Snort
Snort is a network IDS. It matches packets against rules and raises alerts. It does not read the auth log and does not ban by itself.
OpenVAS
OpenVAS is a vulnerability scanner that tests hosts for known weaknesses. It does not watch logs or block addresses.
fail2ban
Right. fail2ban watches log files with filters and adds a temporary firewall rule for addresses that fail too often.
nmap
nmap scans hosts and ports. It does not read logs and it blocks nothing.

q.q: A Snort rule starts with: alert tcp any any -> 10.0.0.5 22. What does the header say?
o: Raise an alert for TCP from any address and port to port 22 on 10.0.0.5
Right. The header has action, protocol, source address and port, direction, destination address and port.
Block all TCP traffic sent from 10.0.0.5 port 22 to every other address
-> means traffic goes TO the right-hand side. alert does not block.
Log all UDP traffic that is sent to 10.0.0.5 on port 22, and ignore TCP
The protocol is tcp, and the action is alert.
Allow SSH from any host and skip other rules
Snort has "pass" for allowing. alert makes an alert.

q.q: A security team wants a tool that tests hosts it is allowed to scan for known vulnerabilities (missing patches, weak settings) using a feed of checks. Which tool fits?
o: Snort (network IDS)
Snort watches traffic for attack signatures. It does not scan hosts for missing patches.
AIDE
AIDE checks file integrity on one host.
Suricata (network IDS)
Suricata is a network IDS/IPS like Snort. It watches traffic and does not run vulnerability checks.
OpenVAS (Greenbone)
Right. OpenVAS is an open-source vulnerability scanner. Only scan systems that you own or have written approval to test.

q.q: Two lab hosts use a simple point-to-point OpenVPN tunnel with a static key (legacy static-key mode). Host A has "ifconfig 10.8.0.1 10.8.0.2" (local, remote). What must host B have?
o: The same line on both sides would give both hosts the same tunnel address.
Right. The first address is the local tunnel end and the second is the remote end, so each side lists them the other way round.
server is for the TLS server mode with many clients, not a static key tunnel.
push "ifconfig 10.8.0.2 10.8.0.1"
push sends options to clients in server mode. It does not work in a static-key setup.

q.q: In a client's OpenVPN config, which directive tells it to act as a client and accept options pushed by the server?
o: This belongs in the server config and defines the VPN address pool.
tls-server
It makes the instance act as the TLS server side. A client must not use it.
dev-node tun0
dev-node names a specific device node and does not make the instance a client.
client
Right. It is shorthand for pull and tls-client. The client then takes routes and addresses from the server.

q.q: A site-to-site tunnel between two offices comes up and the tunnel IPs ping each other, but hosts behind each router cannot reach hosts behind the other. Which two things are most likely missing?
o: Routes for the remote LAN through the tunnel, and IP forwarding on both gateways
Right. The tunnel itself works. Packets for the other LAN need a route to the tunnel, and each gateway must forward packets between its LAN and the tunnel.
A new CA certificate and a fresh Diffie-Hellman file, generated again on both gateways
Certificates would stop the tunnel from coming up, but it is already up.
A bigger MTU on the tun device of each gateway so that LAN frames fit into the tunnel
MTU problems cause hangs on large packets and not total failure of routing.
A second tunnel that uses the tap device for the other direction
tap is for bridging Ethernet and is not a fix for missing routes.

q.q: You must make a remote site part of the SAME Ethernet broadcast domain (so non-IP protocols and DHCP broadcasts cross the tunnel). Which OpenVPN device type do you use?
o: dev tun
tun works at layer 3 and carries only IP packets, so it cannot bridge a broadcast domain.
dev eth0
eth0 is a physical network card, not a VPN device type. OpenVPN uses tun or tap.
dev tap
Right. tap works at layer 2 and carries whole Ethernet frames, so it can be bridged to a LAN.
dev ppp0
OpenVPN uses tun and tap devices, not ppp interfaces.

q.q: Unless you change it, which port and protocol does OpenVPN use by default?
o: UDP 1194
Right. The official default for OpenVPN is port 1194, and UDP is the default protocol (TCP can be chosen).
TCP 443
443 is often chosen to pass strict firewalls, but it is not the default.
UDP 500
Port 500 belongs to IKE, used by IPsec VPNs.
TCP 1723
Port 1723 belongs to PPTP.

q.title: The secondary DNS server does not see the new record
q.scenario: A teammate added the host app to the zone example.test on the primary name server ns1 and reloaded it, but the secondary ns2 (192.0.2.12) still says the name does not exist. Find out why, fix it on ns1 only, and make ns2 pick up the change. Do not restart the name server.

checks.t: Ask ns2 what it knows (its SOA serial or the app record)
checks.why: Start from the symptom. dig @192.0.2.12 shows that ns2 gives NXDOMAIN for app and still holds serial 2026112601. A secondary only answers from the copy it has transferred.

checks.t: Look at the serial on the primary (dig, zone file or zonestatus)
checks.why: ns1 has the same serial, 2026112601, as before the edit. A secondary compares serials: if the primary's number is not higher, it does not transfer the zone, even though the file has a new record.

checks.t: Check the zone file syntax with named-checkzone
checks.why: named-checkzone prints OK, so the file is fine. That rules out a broken zone and points at the serial number.

checks.t: Raise the serial number in the zone file
checks.why: The serial in the SOA record is the version number of the zone. A common style is YYYYMMDDnn, so 2026112701 (or 2026112602) is higher than 2026112601 and tells secondaries that something changed.

checks.t: Reload the zone after raising the serial
checks.why: rndc reload example.test makes ns1 read the file again. ns1 then sends a NOTIFY message to ns2, and ns2 asks for the new zone. A reload before the edit would not help, because the file would still hold the old serial.

checks.t: Check ns2 again after the reload
checks.why: Always prove the fix from the other side. ns2 now shows serial 2026112701 and answers 192.0.2.40 for app. If it does not, give the transfer a few seconds and ask again.

checks.t: Did not restart the name server
checks.why: A restart is not needed. It also empties the cache of a server that may be answering clients, and it hides what really changed. rndc reload does the job without a restart.

q.title: Windows user can open the Samba share but cannot save
q.scenario: On your lab file server fs1, the user alice (member of the Linux group staff) can open the share projects from Windows, but every save fails with 'access denied'. Find the cause, fix it with the smallest change, and make Samba use the change without cutting off other users. Do not open the folder to everyone.
q.ticket: SMB-210: share \\fs1\projects is read only for staff since the weekend rebuild. fs1 is a standalone Samba 4 server (tdbsam) in the lab.

checks.t: Look at how the projects share is set up in Samba
checks.why: testparm shows the settings Samba really uses after defaults are added. The share has 'read only = Yes', which means nobody can write, whatever the Linux permissions say.

checks.t: Check the Linux side: the folder permissions or alice's groups
checks.why: Samba acts as the Linux user, so both layers must allow writing. Here staff owns the folder with rwx and alice is in staff, so the Linux side is fine and the cause is the share setting.

checks.t: Change the share so staff can write
checks.why: Setting 'read only = no' in the [projects] section allows writing for the users the share lets in. 'valid users = @staff' still limits who may connect.

checks.t: Make Samba use the change without a restart
checks.why: smbcontrol all reload-config (or systemctl reload smbd) re-reads smb.conf while users stay connected. The reload must come after the edit, or it re-reads the old file.

checks.t: Show the live setting now says read only = No
checks.why: Look again after the change. testparm now prints 'read only = No', so the share accepts writes.

checks.t: Did not open the folder to everyone with chmod
checks.why: The Linux permissions were already right. chmod 777 would let every local user change the project files and fixes nothing, because the share was read only.

checks.t: Did not restart smbd
checks.why: A restart drops every open file and connection. A reload applies the new setting and leaves other users working.

q.title: Turn off root and password logins without locking yourself out
q.scenario: Change request CR-88 asks you to harden SSH on the lab server labsrv: no direct root login and no password logins. Your own account alice already logs in with a key. Make the changes in the safe order, test the file before you apply it, and prove that key login still works. You have written approval for this change on this server only.
q.ticket: CR-88: sshd hardening on labsrv (lab). Approved by the system owner. Keep your admin session working. Do not lock any account or stop the service.
q.intro: labsrv (Ubuntu 24.04). You are alice with sudo, logged in over SSH. Type help to see the commands.

cmds.out:
total 16
drwx------ 2 alice alice 4096 Nov 12 09:30 .
drwxr-x--- 5 alice alice 4096 Nov 25 14:02 ..
-rw------- 1 alice alice  103 Nov 12 09:30 authorized_keys
-rw-r--r-- 1 alice alice  142 Nov 12 09:31 known_hosts

checks.t: Confirm alice's key is in place before passwords are turned off
checks.why: Do this first. With the key installed (and the .ssh folder and file private to alice), you will still be able to log in after password logins are refused. Without it, you lock yourself out.

checks.t: Stop direct root logins
checks.why: PermitRootLogin no stops anyone logging in as root over SSH. Admins log in as themselves and use sudo, so the log shows who did what.

checks.t: Turn off password logins
checks.why: PasswordAuthentication no removes password guessing as an attack path. Only do it after you know key login works for you.

checks.t: Test the config file with sshd -t after both edits
checks.why: Test AFTER the edits and BEFORE the reload. sshd -t reads the file and prints any error, so a typo cannot lock you out. Also look in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf: drop-in files are read first, and for most keywords the first value wins, so a drop-in can override your edit.

checks.t: Reload sshd only after the test passed
checks.why: A reload (or restart) makes sshd use the new file. Your current session stays open, which is your way back if the change is wrong.

checks.t: Show that key login for alice still works
checks.why: Open a new connection with your key after the change. This is the proof that the change did not lock you out.

checks.t: Show that root and password logins are now refused
checks.why: A refused attempt ('Permission denied (publickey)') proves the new rules are active.

checks.t: Did not stop sshd, lock an account or turn off keys
checks.why: Stopping sshd, locking alice or turning off public keys would cut the way in for the very person doing the change. The ticket asked for a safer SSH, not a closed one.

q.title: Read the Postfix log: why is mail to the partner waiting?
q.scenario: Users say mail to the partner company is slow and some of it has not arrived. Read these lines from /var/log/mail.log on mx1. Mark every line that shows a delivery attempt that did NOT succeed (temporary or permanent), then say what explains most of them.
q.ticket: MAIL-540: messages to partner.example are delayed since 08:30. Mail to other companies is fine.

lines.text: Nov 27 08:41:02 mx1 postfix/smtpd[3150]: connect from workstation12.example.test[10.1.5.12]
lines.why: A client connected to the SMTP server. This is the start of a normal submission and is not a failure.
Alice logged in with SMTP authentication (sasl_username=alice) and Postfix accepted the message into the queue. Our server is doing its job here.

lines.text: Nov 27 08:41:03 mx1 postfix/qmgr[1050]: 7F3D2A1B09: from=<alice@example.test>, size=2411, nrcpt=1 (queue active)
lines.why: The queue manager picked up the message. 'queue active' means Postfix is working on delivering it.

lines.text: Nov 27 08:41:33 mx1 postfix/smtp[3201]: 7F3D2A1B09: to=<tom@partner.example>, relay=mx.partner.example[198.51.100.9]:25, delay=30, delays=0.1/0.02/30/0, dsn=4.4.1, status=deferred (connect to mx.partner.example[198.51.100.9]:25: Connection timed out)
lines.why: status=deferred with 'Connection timed out' means Postfix could not reach the partner's mail server on port 25. dsn=4.4.1 is a temporary (4.x.x) problem, so Postfix keeps the message and tries again later.

lines.text: Nov 27 08:42:10 mx1 postfix/smtp[3204]: 4C9E1D5F20: to=<amy@example.net>, relay=mx.example.net[198.51.100.20]:25, delay=1.2, dsn=2.0.0, status=sent (250 2.0.0 Ok: queued as 8B13E)
lines.why: status=sent and dsn=2.0.0 mean the other server accepted the mail. Mail to example.net works, so our own sending is fine.

lines.text: Nov 27 08:43:15 mx1 postfix/smtp[3207]: 6B7C8D9E0F: to=<kim@partner2.example>, relay=mx2.partner2.example[198.51.100.40]:25, dsn=4.7.1, status=deferred (host mx2.partner2.example[198.51.100.40] said: 451 4.7.1 Greylisted, please try again in 300 seconds)
lines.why: A 451 greylisting reply is a temporary refusal: the partner asks the sender to retry later. The mail was NOT delivered on this attempt, so mark it, but note that it is a different cause from the timeouts and usually clears by itself.

lines.text: Nov 27 08:44:20 mx1 postfix/smtp[3209]: 5E6F7A8B9C: to=<joe@partner.example>, relay=mx.partner.example[198.51.100.9]:25, delay=30, delays=0.1/0.02/30/0, dsn=4.4.1, status=deferred (connect to mx.partner.example[198.51.100.9]:25: Connection timed out)
lines.why: Same host, same timeout, different message. When many messages to one domain show the same deferred error, the cause is the path to that server, not the individual messages.

lines.text: Nov 27 08:45:01 mx1 postfix/smtpd[3150]: disconnect from workstation12.example.test[10.1.5.12] ehlo=2 starttls=1 auth=1 mail=1 rcpt=1 data=1 quit=1 commands=8
lines.why: A clean end of the client session. Every step (STARTTLS, auth, mail, rcpt, data) worked, so the problem is not between the client and our server.

lines.text: Nov 27 08:51:44 mx1 postfix/smtp[3230]: 9A1B2C3D4E: to=<sue@partner.example>, relay=mx.partner.example[198.51.100.9]:25, delay=1230, delays=1200/0.1/30/0, dsn=4.4.1, status=deferred (connect to mx.partner.example[198.51.100.9]:25: Connection timed out)
lines.why: A third deferral to the same server. delay=1230 seconds shows this message has been waiting for about 20 minutes.

lines.text: Nov 27 08:49:30 mx1 postfix/smtp[3220]: 1A2B3C4D5E: to=<old@partner.example>, relay=mx.partner.example[198.51.100.9]:25, dsn=5.1.1, status=bounced (host mx.partner.example[198.51.100.9] said: 550 5.1.1 <old@partner.example>: Recipient address rejected: User unknown)
lines.why: status=bounced with a 550 (5.x.x) is a PERMANENT failure: the address does not exist. It was not delivered, so mark it. It also shows that mx.partner.example answered here, which fits a single wrong address and not a dead server.

lines.text: Nov 27 08:52:09 mx1 postfix/smtp[3236]: 3D4E5F6A7B: to=<ben@example.org>, relay=mx.example.org[203.0.113.25]:25, delay=0.8, dsn=2.0.0, status=sent (250 2.0.0 Ok: queued as 22C70)
lines.why: Delivered. More proof that outgoing mail to other places works.
After a successful delivery the queue manager removes the message from the queue. This is the normal end of a message.

ask.label: What explains most of the failed attempts in this log?
opts: Postfix often cannot connect to mx.partner.example on port 25 (timeouts), so it holds the mail and retries later
Alice's SMTP login to mx1 fails, so the messages never enter the queue and are lost
The recipients tom, joe and sue do not exist at partner.example, so every message bounces back
The partner greylists every sender and asks for a retry after five minutes on each message
mx1 is an open relay and the partner's server refuses its connections for that reason
ask.why: Most failing lines are status=deferred with 'Connection timed out' to mx.partner.example, while mail to other domains is status=sent. The greylisting (451) and the unknown user (550) are one-off lines with their own causes: a temporary retry request and a single wrong address. A login failure would show an authentication error, and the SASL line shows Alice logged in.

q.title: Turn a Linux box into a NAT router for a lab LAN
q.scenario: A Linux machine has eth0 (public side) and eth1 (lab LAN 192.168.10.0/24). The FORWARD chain policy is already DROP. Build the steps that let the LAN reach the Internet through the router and survive a reboot. Put the needed steps in order and leave out the wrong ones.
q.ticket: Lab router LR-1. Interfaces: eth0 = Internet side, eth1 = LAN side. Rules are saved with iptables-save into /etc/iptables/rules.v4 (iptables-persistent).

rules.why: Without IP forwarding the kernel drops packets that are not for the router itself. Writing the setting to a sysctl file AND loading it turns the machine into a router now and after every reboot. (Appending to /etc/sysctl.conf and running sysctl -p does the same.)
This lets packets from the LAN go out to the Internet. With the FORWARD policy on DROP, nothing passes without an accept rule.
This lets the replies come back in. Without it, the LAN can send but the answers are dropped by the DROP policy.
NAT rewrites the private source addresses to the router's public address as packets leave through eth0. POSTROUTING in the nat table is the right place.
Rules in memory are lost at reboot. Saving them last makes sure the file holds the finished set.
This masquerades traffic leaving toward the LAN side (eth1), not toward the Internet. It does nothing for LAN clients going out.
This opens the FORWARD chain for all traffic in every direction, including Internet traffic into the LAN. It removes the protection the DROP policy gives.
This accepts ALL traffic from the Internet into the LAN. Replies are already allowed by the ESTABLISHED,RELATED rule, so this is not needed and it is dangerous.
MASQUERADE is only valid in POSTROUTING. PREROUTING is where destination NAT (DNAT) happens, so this rule is rejected.

last.why: Save only after every rule is in place. Saving earlier would store an incomplete set, and the router would come back from a reboot without NAT.

q.title: Follow one incoming e-mail from the Internet to a phone
q.scenario: A partner sends a message to alice@example.test. Place each part of the mail system in the order the message passes through it, from the sending server to Alice's phone app, which keeps her mail in sync with the server (IMAP).

slots.label: Step 2
slots.zone: Holds the message until it is handled

slots.label: Step 3
slots.zone: Hands the message to the mail store

slots.label: Step 5
slots.zone: Lets the phone read the mailbox

devs.name: Postfix SMTP server (TCP 25)
devs.why: Other mail servers deliver to your domain by SMTP on port 25. Postfix accepts the message, checks the rules (relay, recipient) and queues it.

devs.name: Postfix mail queue
devs.why: Accepted messages wait in the queue until the queue manager can deliver them to the next step.

devs.name: Dovecot LMTP delivery with Sieve
devs.why: Postfix hands the message to Dovecot over LMTP. Dovecot runs the user's Sieve script (for example fileinto) as it delivers.

devs.name: Maildir mailbox of alice
devs.why: The message ends up as a file in Alice's Maildir (or mailbox) on the server.

devs.name: Dovecot IMAP over TLS (TCP 993)
devs.why: Alice's phone logs in to Dovecot with IMAP over TLS and reads the mailbox. The phone never talks to Postfix to read mail.

devs.name: Postfix submission (TCP 587)
devs.why: Submission is the door that Alice's phone uses to SEND mail, after logging in. It is not used for the incoming message.

devs.name: ManageSieve service (TCP 4190)
devs.why: ManageSieve lets users upload and edit their Sieve scripts. The script runs during delivery, but ManageSieve itself carries no mail.

devs.name: BIND zone transfer (AXFR)
devs.why: AXFR copies DNS zones between name servers. It plays no part in delivering a message.

devs.name: Postfix outbound SMTP client
devs.why: The smtp client sends mail OUT to other servers. This message is coming IN, so the first step is the smtpd server that listens on port 25.
